linux-cleanup shows the paths before it removes regenerable caches on Linux. It covers package-manager, browser and build-tool caches, with separate modes for system work and personal-file candidates. Start with a read-only scan or a dry run before choosing a real cleanup. Get linux-cleanup: on npm · the website · all places It is a destructive tool. Every deletion is permanent, and there is no undo. Its safety comes from refusing to touch the wrong things in the first place, not from being able to put them back. This tool deletes files permanently There is no undo, Trash or backup step. Developer machines accumulate an enormous amount of regenerable junk — package-manager caches measured in tens of gigabytes, browser caches, build-tool caches, emulator images, and node_modules for projects abandoned two years ago. Existing cleaners tended to fall into one of two shapes. Either they did not know about modern developer caches at all, or they were single-button wipers that deleted whatever looked like junk and hoped for the best. linux-cleanup takes the opposite stance: scriptable, transparent, allowlist-guarded, and interactive by default. You can read exactly what it will touch before it touches anything.

Fail closed. An allowlist, not a blocklist. A path the tool does not recognise is refused. A blocklist puts one typo between clearing a cache and clearing a home directory. Distinguish caches from tools. ~/.cache/yarn regenerates in seconds; a Gradle wrapper distribution is a 230 MB download you might need next month. The staleness gate exists because treating those the same was wrong, and 1.2.0 changed it. The user is the oracle for personal data. Nothing on disk distinguishes an installer you will never open again from the only copy of a document. The tool refuses to guess, which is why those modes ignore --yes. Prevention over recovery. No undo, by choice — an undo log is write amplification on the disk you are freeing, and it breeds carelessness. Auditable over convenient. Bash, because it is already installed and can be read. A compiled binary would be more ergonomic and much harder to trust. Release checks are narrow. On start, the CLI reads one public release record when online. It does not upload cleanup paths, reports or crash bundles; sending a report remains your choice.

Two of the safety features exist because someone pointed out a real problem. The protected install-root list came from a genuine defect: pnpm cleanup targeted ~/.local/share/pnpm — the install root — and removed globally installed packages. Fixed in 1.1.0, along with an assertion so it cannot recur. The staleness gate came from a user observing that 1.2.0 still wiped Android AVDs wholesale, and that the same reasoning should apply to anything that is a tool rather than a cache. That became 1.2.1. If you find something wrong, say so.

Extends the 1.2.0 staleness gate to anything that is a tool rather than a regenerable cache. Such deletions now require both that no active software depends on the asset and that you have not touched it in --days days.

Android AVDs — previously wiped ~/.android/avd wholesale on confirm. Now each *.avd directory is inspected as a unit, paired with its sibling *.ini, and pruned only when every file in the profile is idle past the threshold. Recently-used emulator profiles survive intact. VS Code / Cursor superseded extensions — the "a newer version exists" check covered the first condition; the superseded directory must now also be idle past the threshold. Recently-loaded older versions are listed but kept, with per-version idle days shown. Flatpak user data — ~/.local/share/flatpak holds installed user-scope apps, not just caches. The module now refuses to touch the tree if any user-scope app is installed, and additionally requires the tree to be idle past the threshold. Points at flatpak uninstall --user --unused for the safer path.

newest_access_age_days <path> — returns days since the freshest atime/mtime anywhere under a path. prune_stale_units <root> <days> [glob] — treats each top-level child as indivisible, so a partial prune cannot corrupt state.

A user pointed out that 1.2.0 still wiped Android AVDs wholesale, and that the same reasoning should apply to anything that is a tool rather than a cache: do not remove software another tool depends on, and do not remove software the user themselves used recently.
The default delete strategy became stale-only. Nothing inside a target cache is removed unless its files have been untouched — both atime and mtime — for --days days, default 100.

clean_target, the shared cleaner behind every cache module, now prunes rather than full-wipes. It deletes only files past the threshold, then sweeps empty directories. Recently-used files survive and the directory shell stays so tools still find their layout. --all-safe prunes per target the same way, and its summary reports bytes freed and bytes kept per target. npm cache cleanup honours the staleness gate instead of always running npm cache clean --force, which ignored age entirely. The pre-run banner states the active strategy — "prune ≥Nd" or "FULL PURGE".

--purge-all restores pre-1.2.0 wipe-everything behaviour, documented with the trade-off spelled out. prune_stale <root> <days> — a public helper for modules that refuses protected paths, deletes only where both timestamps exceed the threshold, sweeps empty directories, and reports bytes freed.

The 1.1.0 default deleted whole cache trees on confirm. That was right for ~/.cache/yarn, which regenerates quickly, and wrong for ~/.gradle/wrapper/dists/ — a 230 MB download you might genuinely need next month. A 100-day threshold cleanly separates "I touched this recently and would miss it" from "I have not opened this in three months". Power users can still force the old behaviour or sharpen the gate with -d 30.
Safety-hardening release. Closes the door on globally installed packages and shell-init files ever being touched.

pnpm globals were being wiped. Cleanup of the pnpm content store targeted ~/.local/share/pnpm (PNPM_HOME) — which holds globally installed packages, bin shims, and the pnpm binary itself from pnpm setup. It now targets only ~/.local/share/pnpm/store, the regenerable content-addressable cache. Affected --all-safe, menu option 3, scan, walkthrough and --list-targets.

PROTECTED_EXACT — an exact-match block on package-manager install directories and runtime homes: pnpm, npm, yarn, bun, deno, volta, nvm, fnm, cargo, rustup and Go. PROTECTED_BASENAMES — refuses any path whose basename is a shell-init or history file, regardless of its location. An --all-safe startup assertion that aborts with a BUG: message if any protected runtime directory ever leaks into the target list, preventing a silent regression.
bun: cache cleanup at ~/.bun/install/cache; ~/.bun/install/global protected. deno: cache cleanup at ~/.cache/deno; ~/.deno/bin protected. Both wired into --all-safe, --scan and the new globals audit.

--globals — a read-only audit listing directly-installed global packages from npm, pnpm, yarn, bun and deno, marking each recently used, needed by: <pkg>, or STALE — safe to uninstall, and printing copy-pasteable uninstall commands. Never deletes anything. Works even when the package manager CLI is not on PATH. --doctor — detects a runtime present on disk but not wired into shell init (nvm, pnpm, bun, deno, cargo) and offers to append the canonical block. Appends only, with confirmation. Never deletes or modifies existing lines.
--all-safe prints explicit "globals are PRESERVED" and "shell-init files are NEVER touched" notices.
Initial public release.

Published to npm — runnable via npx linux-cleanup or npm install -g linux-cleanup. The package ships a thin Node launcher that locates the bash entry point and routes logs and records to ~/.linux-cleanup/ so they survive npx temp eviction. Direct git clone also supported, keeping output inside the clone.

Guided ten-step walkthrough as the default mode, with progress headers, a / s / q prompts, per-step bytes-freed display and a running total. Allowlist-based safety — refuses any path inside a curated protected list, plus bare $HOME and /. Personal data interactive-only — never batched, never --yes-able. Cleanup categories — package-manager caches (yarn, npm, pnpm, pip, composer); application caches (Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Chromium, Edge, Vivaldi, Gradle, Cypress, Playwright, TypeScript, Zoom); developer tools (Android AVDs, pub-cache, Dart, flatpak); editor extensions; stale node_modules; partial downloads and stale personal files; system cleanup under sudo. Session records — canonical JSON written every run, with on-demand Markdown and HTML export. HTML uses dark-mode-aware embedded CSS. Reports manager (--reports) and non-interactive --export FMT ID. Self-test (--self-test) verifying dependencies, the syntax of every shell file, and safety-guard sanity — asserting protection returns true for /, $HOME, ~/Documents and /etc. --feedback and --debug-bundle for structured bug reporting. Privacy — zero network calls. No telemetry, analytics or crash reporting. The only data that leaves your machine is what you choose to email. Credits in every artefact — logs open with a self-attributing header, records carry a top-level credits block, HTML output is footer-credited. Setup helpers — --install-alias, --install-cron and their uninstall counterparts. NO_COLOR support and --no-color.

HTML output escapes all JSON-derived values through jq's @html filter, preventing injection from a malformed record. command -v guards on every optional dependency (snap, crontab, xdg-open, jq). realpath -m resolves symlinks before any protected-path check, so a symlink cannot evade the allowlist.

Every cleanup in the desktop app takes the same four steps, in the same order. Nothing can skip one.

The first time the app opens it shows three short steps: what the app is, which folders the CLI always refuses, and an optional Sign in with Google. Each can be skipped and opened again from Help. Signing in is never needed to clean up; it adds real runs to the month and keeps run numbers across your computers (Accounts and plans). Sign-in opens Google in your browser. Start a dry run runs the all-safe cleanup with --dry-run. It removes nothing, anywhere. The screen then lists every path the cleanup would remove, its measured size and why, and every path the CLI refused and kept, with the reason. Save the list as JSON writes that list to a file on this computer. A dashed button in the app is always a dry run. A solid button removes files.

Review and run opens the only screen that starts a real run. It repeats what the dry run found, says how many real runs your plan has left this month, and states that removal is permanent. Run the cleanup now stays unavailable while: the dry run is more than a day old (run it again first); another run is still going; no real runs are left this month.

The CLI reports each path as it removes it, and the screen follows along. It checks every path again before it removes it, so something that changed since the dry run is judged as it is now. Cancel after this item stops once the current step finishes; anything already removed stays removed.

Every run ends with a receipt, a dry run included: free space before and after, each step marked completed, skipped or failed, and how the run ended. A cancelled or interrupted run lists its unfinished step as failed. Receipts stay on this computer under Receipts & history, beside the CLI's own reports and logs in ~/.linux-cleanup/. The app updates itself. It checks for a signed update when it starts, when its window comes back into view, and the moment a new release is published. With Install updates automatically on (the default), it downloads the update, checks its signature, and relaunches at a quiet moment: never while a run is in progress. An AppImage is replaced in place. A .deb install updates through dpkg, so your desktop asks for an administrator password first (the usual graphical prompt); cancelling it leaves the current version running. A release can also be marked required: an urgent release stops the app at once, says why, and offers one Update button; a normal release says that a new version is out, and from the next start it is required. If the app is offline when it checks, it carries on; a check that fails never blocks a run.

The desktop app is linux-cleanup in a window. It bundles the same CLI this site documents and runs one mode through it: the all-safe cleanup, first as a dry run, then as a real run when you confirm. Every rule about what is removed and what is refused belongs to the CLI; the app shows those decisions and never edits them.

The app starts the bundled cleanup.sh with one of exactly two argument lists and reads its --json-events stream: You press The app runs Start a dry run --all-safe --yes --dry-run --json-events Run the cleanup now --all-safe --yes --json-events Reports and logs go to ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/ and ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/, the same folders an npx linux-cleanup run uses, so the app and the terminal share one history. The bundled copy skips the CLI's own update check (LINUX_CLEANUP_LAUNCHER=desktop). The app checks for its own updates instead; see Install and update.

Data Leaves the computer? File and folder paths, file names Never Step results, sizes, free space before and after, the distribution name Only when you sign in, as numbers Which screens open and which actions run Counted with Amplitude, without paths, names or your email Signing in is optional. Signed out, dry runs, real runs, receipts and schedules all work on this computer; the monthly real-run allowance is counted per computer.

A real run removes files the way the CLI does: permanently, with no copy kept. The app asks for a recent dry run before a real run, and the confirm screen says this in plain words before anything runs.

Schedules are part of the Pro and Team plans. A schedule is a pair of systemd user units in ~/.config/systemd/user/, named linux-cleanup-schedule-<id>.timer and .service. It runs either a dry run or the all-safe cleanup, daily, weekly or on a day of the month (1 to 28). The timer uses Persistent=true: if the computer was off at the set time, the run happens at the next login. Each scheduled run writes its event stream to ~/.linux-cleanup/schedule-runs/, and the app turns it into a receipt the next time you open it. Because an AppImage's files disappear when the app closes, a schedule runs a copy of the bundled CLI in ~/.linux-cleanup/desktop-engine/. The app refreshes that copy whenever it starts, so a timer always runs the version the app ships. To see or stop a timer from a terminal: systemctl --user list-timers 'linux-cleanup-schedule-*' systemctl --user disable --now linux-cleanup-schedule-<id>.timer
The app's Help › Errors & offline screen covers the same cases with a button for each. This page is the long form.

Nothing happens on double-click. The file needs to be executable: chmod +x linux-cleanup_*_amd64.AppImage. An error mentions FUSE. AppImages mount themselves with FUSE 2. Ubuntu 22.04 and later do not install it by default: sudo apt install libfuse2 (on Ubuntu 24.04, libfuse2t64). Without it, the AppImage can also run as ./linux-cleanup_*_amd64.AppImage --appimage-extract-and-run. An error mentions WebKitGTK or libwebkit2gtk-4.1. The window needs WebKitGTK 4.1 from your distribution. On Debian and Ubuntu, the .deb pulls it in; with the AppImage, install libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0.

The app checks its own copy of cleanup.sh at start. If that check fails, the installation is damaged: download the release again from the download page. Your receipts, reports and logs are not touched by a reinstall.
documents.s: The app says the bundled CLI is missing

documents.t: Sign-in runs in your browser and returns to the app through 127.0.0.1. If the browser shows the result but the app does not move on, a firewall or a browser extension may be blocking local addresses. Nothing changes on a failed sign-in; Sign in with Google can be pressed again.

Dry runs, real runs, receipts and schedules never need the internet. Offline, the app keeps counting real runs against this computer's monthly pool and syncs when the server answers again. Only plan changes and synced history wait.

documents.t: systemctl --user list-timers 'linux-cleanup-schedule-*' journalctl --user -u 'linux-cleanup-schedule-*' --since today A timer fires only while you are logged in; one missed while the computer was off runs at the next login. Each run that did start leaves its stream in ~/.linux-cleanup/schedule-runs/, and the app turns it into a receipt when you next open it.

Schedules are systemd user timers, and they run a copy of the CLI outside the app. Removing the app does not remove them. Delete each one on the Schedules screen before you uninstall, or from a terminal: systemctl --user disable --now 'linux-cleanup-schedule-*.timer' rm -f ~/.config/systemd/user/linux-cleanup-schedule-*.{timer,service} systemctl --user daemon-reload
Installed as Remove with AppImage Delete the .AppImage file .deb sudo apt remove linux-cleanup

Folder Holds Remove it if ~/.linux-cleanup/ Reports, logs, scheduled-run streams and the schedules' CLI copy. The terminal CLI uses the same folder You no longer use the CLI either ~/.local/share/com.aoneahsan.linuxcleanup/ The app's settings, receipts and this computer's random device id Always safe to remove after uninstalling A signed-in account lives on after the app is gone. Home cache cleanup is designed for Linux distributions with the required GNU utilities. --system uses Debian and Ubuntu package commands. Check the installed tools with --self-test before cleanup.

Distro family $HOME cache cleanup --system Debian, Ubuntu, Mint, Pop!_OS Full Full Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Alma With required utilities Do not use: apt steps fail Arch, Manjaro, EndeavourOS With required utilities Do not use: apt steps fail openSUSE With required utilities Do not use: apt steps fail Alpine, minimal containers Needs Bash and GNU utilities Do not use: apt steps fail WSL With required utilities Debian/Ubuntu only; inspect mounted paths first --system has no distro detection The apt steps call apt and dpkg directly, with no command -v guard and no fallback to dnf, pacman or zypper. On a non-Debian system they fail with "command not found" per step. The mode does not abort after an apt failure: later steps can still run. Avoid it on other distributions. Some descriptions of this tool claim graded multi-distro support for --system, with dnf substituting for apt and paccache on Arch. No such code exists. Verify with grep -rn 'dnf\|pacman\|zypper' modules/system_sudo.sh on a clone — it returns nothing.

--system step Debian/Ubuntu Fedora/RHEL Arch openSUSE apt autoremove + apt clean Works Fails Fails Fails journalctl --vacuum-size=100M Works Works Works Works Disabled snap revisions Works If snap installed If snap installed If snap installed Kernel listing (dpkg --list) Works Silent — prints nothing Silent Silent /tmp files older than 7 days Works Works Works Works Page-cache drop Works Works Works Works The journal, /tmp and page-cache steps rely on journalctl, find and sysctl, which behave the same everywhere systemd is present. The kernel step is listing-only regardless, so its failure on non-dpkg systems costs nothing.

On a non-Debian system, use its package manager's own maintenance guidance. The commands below are examples to review before running: # Fedora / RHEL / Rocky sudo dnf autoremove sudo dnf clean all # Arch / Manjaro (paccache is in pacman-contrib) sudo pacman -Rns "$(pacman -Qtdq)" # orphans, if any sudo paccache -r # keep the last 3 versions sudo pacman -Scc # clear the whole package cache # openSUSE sudo zypper clean --all sudo zypper packages --orphaned For home caches, preview what linux-cleanup finds: linux-cleanup --scan linux-cleanup --all-safe --dry-run

Home paths come from the installed tools rather than the distribution. Availability varies by machine: Package-manager caches — yarn, npm, pnpm, pip, composer, bun, deno Browser caches — Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Chromium, Edge, Vivaldi Build-tool caches — Gradle, Cypress, Playwright, TypeScript Developer-tool data — Android AVDs, Flutter pub-cache, Dart, flatpak Editor extensions — VS Code, Cursor node_modules, partial downloads, personal stale files Scan, audit, safety checks and local logs

Alpine and other minimal images typically ship BusyBox rather than GNU coreutils. The tool needs GNU find, du, stat and especially realpath — the last is what resolves symlinks before the protected-path check. apk add coreutils findutils bash linux-cleanup --self-test --self-test names the first missing dependency. Do not run destructive modes until it passes.

The tool runs in the Linux environment. Its path guard resolves symlinks, but it does not identify Windows personal folders as protected Linux folders. Inspect the scan and dry run carefully if your home directories or caches point into /mnt/.
Not supported. The npm package declares "os": ["linux"] and will refuse to install. Paths, find flags and package managers all differ.
System cleanup — the mode this page qualifies Requirements
Symptom-specific problems belong in Troubleshooting; design rationale is in Safety guards.

Your source files, no. ~/Documents and the other personal directories are protected outright, and no cleanup target points at a project's source. The closest it comes is finding stale node_modules directories inside your project roots. Those are interactive-only with per-project confirmation, and yarn install rebuilds them. One caveat worth knowing: if you edited a file inside node_modules directly, rather than through a patch tool, that edit exists nowhere else.

The CLI checks a public release record over HTTPS at start when online. It sends no scan results, cleanup paths or crash bundle. Offline, the check fails open and the run continues. Verify it yourself on a clone: grep -rE 'curl|wget|http://|https://' cleanup.sh lib/ modules/ bin/ The release check lives in modules/update_check.sh; inspect that file too. Installing or accepting an update uses npm or GitHub. The feedback helper opens a draft that you choose whether to send.

An undo log would be write amplification on the disk you are trying to free — keeping 20 GB in order to reclaim 20 GB accomplishes nothing. It would also create false confidence, and be partial at best. The safety model is prevention instead: an allowlist, a staleness gate, and interactive confirmation. Full reasoning: Deletion is permanent.

Yes. --scan reads only; --dry-run walks the selected cleanup without deleting files or changing settings. A dry run still keeps a local log and writes no JSON session report. See Preview before deleting.

linux-cleanup --self-test # verifies the guards actually fire linux-cleanup --scan # read-only; shows what would be reclaimed linux-cleanup --list-targets # every path it can touch linux-cleanup --all-safe --dry-run # preview a cache cleanup After those three you have seen the safety model work without losing a byte. Then run linux-cleanup and answer n to anything that surprises you.
documents.s: What is the safest way to try it?

documents.t: A little, sometimes, and it is worth being honest about how little: VS Code launches faster with a dozen extension directories rather than fifty A cold cache is marginally faster to skim than a bloated one Browser cold-starts are unaffected — caches are key-value, lookups are O(1) The page-cache drop frees RAM, not disk, and the kernel refills it immediately The real benefit is that "disk full" stops blocking your work — not a benchmark number.
documents.s: Will it speed up my computer?

documents.t: The current removal finishes — usually well under a second — then the script exits with code 130. The log keeps everything up to that point. The crash trap deliberately ignores 130, so no crash bundle is written.
documents.s: What if I press Ctrl-C mid-cleanup?

documents.t: You can, but you should not. It is designed to run as a normal user, and running as root only widens the blast radius if a bug ever slipped past the guards. --system handles the legitimate sudo needs internally, one audited command at a time.
documents.s: Can I run it as root?

documents.t: Cache cleanup inside $HOME works on every Linux distribution. --system is Debian and Ubuntu only — it calls apt and dpkg with no distro detection. On Fedora, Arch or openSUSE its package steps fail while the journal, /tmp and page-cache steps still work. See Distro support.
documents.s: Does it work on my distro?

documents.t: The CLI runs on the Linux side. Review any symlink from your Linux home into /mnt/c/ before cleanup. The allowlist resolves symlinks, but a Windows Documents path is not automatically covered by a Linux home-path rule.

Bash is already on every system this targets. A compiled binary would mean shipping something users cannot easily audit; a Python or Node implementation would add a runtime dependency to a tool whose entire job is removing things from your disk. The script is a few thousand lines of commented bash that a senior engineer can read in an afternoon. For a tool that runs rm -rf with sudo available, auditability is worth more than ergonomics.
documents.s: Why bash rather than Python, Go or Rust?

documents.t: Mode Cadence --scan Monthly, as a baseline --all-safe -y Weekly — automate it --system Quarterly, manually --node-modules Yearly, once side projects pile up --editor-ext When the editor feels slow — also covered by --all-safe --stale Quarterly, deliberately --doctor When command not found appears --globals Before reinstalling Node or migrating machines
documents.s: How often should I run it?

documents.t: It disables the staleness gate, wiping caches in full rather than pruning idle files. That includes Gradle wrapper distributions, Playwright browsers and Cypress binaries you might still want. It is the right choice before reimaging a machine and a poor default otherwise. Never combine it with a cron job.

linux-cleanup ships three ways: npx with no install, a global npm install, or a git clone. All three run the same Bash script — the npm package is a thin Node launcher that locates cleanup.sh and points logs and reports at a persistent directory. Check the installed version Run linux-cleanup --version after installation or upgrade. The changelog records changes to the dry run and release notices.

The fastest way to evaluate it. Nothing lands on your PATH and nothing is left behind if you decide against it. npx linux-cleanup --version npx linux-cleanup --scan # read-only audit npx linux-cleanup # guided walkthrough npx fetches the package into a temporary npm cache directory. Your logs and reports are written to ~/.linux-cleanup/ — not the temp directory — so they survive npm cache eviction and are still there next time.

npm install -g linux-cleanup linux-cleanup --version linux-cleanup is then on your PATH everywhere. Logs and reports still go to ~/.linux-cleanup/. npm install -g linux-cleanup@latest # upgrade npm uninstall -g linux-cleanup # remove Uninstalling the package does not remove a shell alias or cron entry you installed — see Uninstall for the complete removal.

For reading the source, auditing it, or modifying it. The repository contents are what npm publishes. git clone https://github.com/aoneahsan/linux-cleanup ~/linux-cleanup cd ~/linux-cleanup chmod +x cleanup.sh ./cleanup.sh --self-test ./cleanup.sh The one behavioural difference: a clone keeps its output alongside the source, in <clone>/logs/, <clone>/reports/ and <clone>/feedback/, rather than in ~/.linux-cleanup/. Both are overridable with LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME. See Output paths. The project is MIT licensed, so forks and modifications are fine.

linux-cleanup --version # confirms which build you actually have linux-cleanup --self-test # dependency, syntax and safety-guard checks A clean self-test ends with a pass message. It asserts that the protected-path guard really does refuse /, $HOME, ~/Documents, ~/.ssh and /etc, and that it does not refuse ~/.cache/yarn. Any failed assertion exits non-zero. Run --self-test after every upgrade It is the only check that runs against the code you actually have rather than against documentation. It takes a second.
documents.s: Verify before you run anything destructive

documents.t: If you… Use Want to try it once npx Will run it regularly, or from cron Global npm install Want to read or modify the source git clone Are on a machine without Node.js git clone Need output kept next to the source git clone For cron specifically, prefer a global install and use an absolute path in the crontab — cron runs with a minimal PATH and will not find a ~/.local/bin install. This is the single most common cron problem; see Alias and cron.

No system service, no background daemon, no scheduled task (until you ask for one) No telemetry agent. On start, the CLI fetches one public release record when online; it continues when offline No shell configuration changes unless you run --install-alias or --doctor No files outside the package and ~/.linux-cleanup/, and the latter only once you actually run it
Quick start — your first cleanup What it deletes — read before the first destructive run Uninstall — complete removal, including alias and cron

Verify the guards, inspect the scan, and preview the selected mode before deleting. Space recovered depends on the paths and files on this machine. Do not skip steps 1 and 2 They take two minutes and they are the difference between a cleanup you controlled and one you discovered afterwards. This tool deletes permanently.

npx linux-cleanup --version npx linux-cleanup --self-test --version confirms which build you have. --self-test checks dependencies, shell syntax, and asserts the safety guards actually fire. A clean run ends with a pass message; any failed assertion exits non-zero and you should stop there.

npx linux-cleanup --scan --scan is read-only. It lists cache roots and their current sizes, along with other candidates and system observations. It does not delete or write a JSON session report. Read the paths before continuing. A cache root's size is not a claim that the whole directory is eligible for removal. Check any unexpected path and each personal-file candidate separately.

npx linux-cleanup --all-safe --dry-run This walks the all-safe cache mode without deleting files or changing settings. Read the proposed actions, then choose whether to run it. A real deletion has no undo.

npx linux-cleanup No flags means the guided walkthrough: ten steps, each asking before it does anything, with a running total of bytes reclaimed. At each step you get three choices: Key Effect a Run this step (the default — pressing Enter chooses it) s Skip this step q Quit the walkthrough now Inside a step, individual targets get their own [Y/n] confirmation. So there are two levels: skip a whole category, or accept the category and decline specific items. The ten steps, in order: Package-manager caches Application caches Developer-tool data Editor old extensions Stale node_modules Partial / orphan downloads Personal stale files System cleanup (sudo) Final size audit Generate readable report Steps 6 and 7 are the ones to slow down on Everything before them is regenerable. Partial downloads and personal stale files are not — read each candidate rather than accepting the batch. Skip both with s on a first run if you would rather review them separately later. Ctrl-C stops the walkthrough with code 130. Any earlier deletion remains permanent. Read the log to see which steps ran before the interruption.

The session ends with a summary naming its log and, when generated, its report. Read the named paths from your own run rather than assuming a fixed location for every install method. The guided walkthrough writes a JSON report unless you pass --no-report or --dry-run. To convert an existing report for reading or archiving, install jq and run: linux-cleanup --export both latest # Markdown + HTML beside the JSON linux-cleanup --reports # interactive reports manager See Reports.

Only after a manual run you were happy with: linux-cleanup --install-alias # type `cleanup` from anywhere linux-cleanup --install-cron # weekly --all-safe -y, Sundays at 03:00 The cron job runs --all-safe -y, which auto-confirms regenerable caches only. It cannot touch personal files — --yes is ignored by those modes. See Alias and cron for exactly what each writes and how to remove it.

linux-cleanup runs on Linux with bash 4 or newer and GNU coreutils. Everything else is optional and degrades gracefully when missing.

Operating system Linux only. The npm package declares "os": ["linux"] and will refuse to install elsewhere Shell bash ≥ 4.0 Node.js ≥ 14 — only for the npx and npm install -g paths. Not needed for a git clone Privileges Runs as a normal user. Only --system requests sudo macOS and WSL are worth separating: macOS is not supported. The paths, find flags and package managers differ. A sibling tool exists for it; do not point this one at a Mac. WSL runs on the Linux side. Review any symlink from $HOME into /mnt/c/ before a cleanup. The allowlist resolves symlinks, but its protected Linux home paths do not imply that every Windows directory is protected.

These are present on essentially every mainstream distro. bash, find, du, df, rm, awk, sort, grep, sed, stat, realpath. realpath matters more than the others: it is what resolves symlinks before the protected-path check. On a minimal container image without GNU coreutils, install them before running. npx linux-cleanup --self-test --self-test probes every required command and names the first one missing, with a fix hint. Run it before anything destructive.

Each unlocks one feature. Without it, that feature is unavailable and the rest of the tool is unaffected. Dependency Unlocks Without it jq Markdown / HTML report export JSON reports still written; conversion unavailable whiptail The visual TUI menu --tui falls back to the CLI menu with an install hint dialog TUI fallback when whiptail is absent As above snap Disabled snap-revision cleanup in --system That step is skipped cleanly crontab The weekly cron installer --install-cron cannot run numfmt Human-readable byte sizes Falls back to raw byte counts xdg-open Opening HTML reports in a browser Open the file manually less Paged JSON view in the reports manager Read the file directly lsb_release Better distro detection in feedback bundles Bundle still generated

jq (report export) and whiptail (visual menu) are the two most people want. # Debian / Ubuntu / Mint sudo apt install jq whiptail # Fedora / RHEL / Rocky sudo dnf install jq newt # Arch / Manjaro sudo pacman -S jq libnewt # openSUSE sudo zypper install jq newt The whiptail binary ships in the newt package on RPM-based distros and libnewt on Arch.

Cache cleanup inside $HOME — which is the large majority of what this tool reclaims — works identically on every Linux distribution. --system is Debian/Ubuntu only The sudo mode calls apt and dpkg directly, with no distro detection and no guard. On Fedora, Arch or openSUSE its package steps fail with "command not found". Full breakdown of which steps work where: Distro support.

Each run can write a local log. A guided walkthrough can also write a JSON report, and a debug bundle is created when requested or after an unexpected failure. Their size depends on the run. See Output paths for the layout.
Installation — the three install paths Quick start — your first cleanup
Two one-time setup helpers: a cleanup shell alias, and a weekly automated run. Both are reversible with a matching uninstall flag. linux-cleanup --install-alias linux-cleanup --install-cron

linux-cleanup --install-alias Appends a cleanup alias to ~/.bash_aliases or ~/.zshrc, depending on your shell. Afterwards, typing cleanup anywhere runs the tool. Reload your shell or the alias will not appear to exist: source ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc Remove it with linux-cleanup --uninstall-alias. Shell-init files are protected at the deletion layer .bashrc, .zshrc, .bash_aliases and similar are on the protected-basename list, so no cleanup mode can ever delete one — regardless of the path it appears at. The alias installer appends; the uninstaller removes only its own line.
linux-cleanup --install-cron Schedules --all-safe -y for Sundays at 03:00, appending output to ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log. Requires crontab. Remove it with linux-cleanup --uninstall-cron.

It is the only mode --yes applies to, and it cannot touch personal data — the interactive-only modes are not part of it and ignore --yes by design. So an unattended run can clear caches and can never delete a file from ~/Downloads. See Guard 3. The staleness gate still applies, so recently-used files survive each weekly pass.
documents.s: Why --all-safe is the right mode for this

documents.t: For a different schedule or flags: crontab -e 0 3 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --no-report --cleanup-logs >>~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log 2>&1 Use an absolute path Cron runs with a minimal PATH — typically just /usr/bin:/bin. A bare linux-cleanup will not be found if it lives in ~/.local/bin or a Node version-manager directory, and the job fails silently every week. This is the most common problem with scheduled runs. Find your path with: command -v linux-cleanup Or set PATH= explicitly at the top of the crontab. Flag Why in cron --all-safe -y Unattended, caches only --no-report Stops JSON records accumulating — they are never auto-deleted --cleanup-logs Removes that run's log at the end -d 30 Optional: more aggressive weekly pruning --cleanup-logs alone is not enough to keep the directory small: it never touches records. --no-report is the flag that does. Do not add --purge-all to a scheduled job Unattended plus no staleness gate means an expensive asset can disappear the week before you need it, with nobody watching. Keep --purge-all for deliberate, supervised runs. See Reclaim the most space.

tail -100 ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log crontab -l | grep -i cleanup If the log shows command not found, it is the PATH problem above. If the log is empty, the job never fired — check that the cron daemon is running (systemctl status cron or crond). The cron log is never rotated. Rotate it yourself when it grows: mv ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log.old touch ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log

If you prefer timers to cron, there is nothing tool-specific about it — schedule the same command. The tool neither knows nor cares which scheduler invoked it, and --install-cron is a convenience rather than a requirement.
linux-cleanup --uninstall-alias linux-cleanup --uninstall-cron Full removal including the package itself: Uninstall.
Measure first. Choose the smallest cleanup scope that addresses the paths you found. A reported cache-root size is not a promise that a cleanup can or should remove all of it.

linux-cleanup --audit linux-cleanup --scan --audit lists large entries in $HOME, including things this tool cannot clean. --scan lists configured cache roots and other candidates without deleting. If a VM image, dataset or game library is the main use of disk, inspect it directly instead of running unrelated cleanup modes.

linux-cleanup --all-safe --dry-run The default all-safe mode prunes eligible regenerable caches after the 100-day idle threshold. The preview walks those rules without deleting. A local log and update-check state may still be written. If every proposed path is one you can rebuild or download again, run linux-cleanup --all-safe and review its confirmation. --yes is for an unattended run after you have already reviewed this machine.

linux-cleanup --node-modules --dry-run The project dependency mode is interactive. Check the project path and its lockfile before a real deletion. A local change made inside node_modules is not restored by reinstalling dependencies.

linux-cleanup --system --dry-run The full system mode uses apt and dpkg, so it is for Debian and Ubuntu. It requests sudo and includes a journal vacuum, aged /tmp files and an optional page-cache step. The page-cache step affects RAM, not disk. See System cleanup.

--days N changes which idle files or whole cache units qualify. Lowering it from 100 to 30 can remove material you used recently, so inspect a dry run with the chosen value first. --purge-all disables the age guard; it can remove a Gradle distribution or test browser you will need to download again.
documents.s: 5. Change the age threshold only after another preview

documents.t: --stale shows large idle personal-file candidates and asks for each deletion. An old download may be your only copy. --yes does not approve this mode. See Stale personal files and Deletion is permanent. The space recovered varies by machine and by other processes writing during the run. Inspect the final log and the paths kept before deciding whether another mode is needed.
documents.s: 6. Keep personal files as a separate decision

documents.t: Two commands produce everything a maintainer needs. Nothing is transmitted automatically — you review the bundle and send it yourself. linux-cleanup --debug-bundle # package the latest log + session record linux-cleanup --feedback # instructions, and an optional mailto draft

linux-cleanup --debug-bundle Writes ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/debug-bundle-<timestamp>.tar.gz containing: The latest session log The latest JSON session record, if one exists A MANIFEST.txt with distro, kernel, bash version and self-test output Then: linux-cleanup --feedback Prints what to include and offers to open a pre-filled mailto: draft with system information already completed.

A bundle contains paths from your machine Not file contents — but the log names every path touched, which means directory names, project names, and sometimes filenames from ~/Downloads. Inspect it first: tar -tzf ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/debug-bundle-*.tar.gz # list contents tar -xzOf ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/debug-bundle-*.tar.gz # read it in full If something in there is sensitive, extract the bundle, remove or redact the file, and re-archive — or just send the manifest plus the specific lines that matter.
documents.s: Review the bundle before sending it

documents.t: Since 1.3.0, an unexpected non-zero exit writes crash-<timestamp>.tar.gz to the same directory automatically, and prints the path. It holds the active log, the most recent record, and a system manifest including the exit code. The bundle is not uploaded. The release check reads a public text file, but it does not send a bundle or local paths. The bundle stays on your disk until you decide whether to share it. Crash bundles are not written for expected exits: 0, 130 (Ctrl-C), 143 (SIGTERM) and 2 (argument error) are all excluded. See Exit codes.

A good report is short and specific: Include Example Distro and version lsb_release -d Bash version bash --version | head -1 Tool version linux-cleanup --version The exact command linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -d 30 Expected versus actual "expected the Gradle wrapper kept, it was deleted" The bundle Attach the tar.gz The most valuable line is expected versus actual. A log alone shows what happened but not why you think it was wrong.

Route Use for GitHub issues Bugs, feature requests — preferred, public aoneahsan@gmail.com Anything you would rather not post publicly A pull request You have a fix. MIT licensed, forks welcome Feature requests by description are as welcome as code. Say what you would want cleaned and why the existing modes do not cover it.

Anything contradicting the documented safety model: A deletion inside a protected path A current editor extension version removed, not just a superseded one A file deleted despite being newer than --days, without --purge-all A personal-data mode acting without confirmation A network request that sends local cleanup paths or reports Each of those is a safety-model violation rather than an inconvenience.

Release check and local reports At start, linux-cleanup reads one public release record over HTTPS when online. It does not upload scans, logs or crash bundles. Installing or updating a copy uses npm or GitHub. Verify on a clone: grep -rE 'curl|wget|http://|https://' cleanup.sh lib/ modules/ bin/ Read modules/update_check.sh for the release request and the command offered for a newer copy. Logs, records and bundles are local files. The maintainer cannot see them, and cannot push a fix to your machine — a new version reaches you when you re-run npx or upgrade.
Troubleshooting — check here first Recovery — if data was lost Exit codes
Remove the automation first, then the package, then the data. Uninstalling the package does not remove a shell alias or cron entry you installed — those are separate.

linux-cleanup --uninstall-alias linux-cleanup --uninstall-cron Do this before removing the package, while the command still exists. If you have already removed it, see manual removal below. Verify: crontab -l | grep -i cleanup # expect no output grep -rn 'cleanup' ~/.bash_aliases ~/.zshrc 2>/dev/null

npm uninstall -g linux-cleanup For npx, nothing is installed — the npm cache evicts it on its own. To clear it now: npm cache clean --force For a git clone, delete the directory: rm -rf ~/linux-cleanup A clone holds its own logs and records Unlike the npm install paths, a clone keeps output in <clone>/logs/ and <clone>/reports/. Deleting the clone deletes those too. Copy anything you want to keep first. See Output paths.

Logs, session records and feedback bundles live in ~/.linux-cleanup/ and are never removed by uninstalling. ls -la ~/.linux-cleanup/ # look before deleting rm -rf ~/.linux-cleanup/ They are small — usually a few megabytes — and they are the only account of what past runs deleted. Keeping them costs nothing; removing them is irreversible like anything else. If you set LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME, remove that directory instead, and drop the export from your shell configuration.
rm -f ~/.config/personal-roots.txt ~/.config/project-roots.txt Only present if you created them. See Environment variables.

documents.t: Undo both helpers by hand. Cron: crontab -e # delete the line containing linux-cleanup or cleanup.sh Alias: grep -n 'cleanup' ~/.bash_aliases ~/.zshrc 2>/dev/null Remove the matching alias line with your editor, then source the file or open a new terminal.
documents.s: If you removed the package first

documents.t: Nothing, once the above is done. The tool installs no system service, no daemon, no systemd unit, no /etc entry and no root-owned file. Everything it creates is inside your home directory. Effects on your system it does not undo — because they are not files it owns: Deleted caches stay deleted. They regenerate as each tool needs them Shell-init blocks added by --doctor stay. They are the correct configuration for runtimes you have installed; remove them by hand if you want them gone
command -v linux-cleanup # expect no output crontab -l | grep -i cleanup # expect no output ls ~/.linux-cleanup 2>&1 # expect: No such file or directory
Installation — if you are reinstalling

--all-safe cleans every regenerable cache in a single pass. It is the mode for unattended maintenance and the only mode --yes applies to. linux-cleanup --all-safe # one confirmation for the batch linux-cleanup --all-safe -y # no prompts — the cron form

Safe means regenerable: package-manager caches, browser and application caches, and stale developer-tool data. It does not mean risk-free, and it does not mean reversible — deletions are still permanent. What --all-safe will never touch, regardless of --yes: Personal files in ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop or anywhere else Partial downloads node_modules directories Anything on the protected-path list Globally installed packages or shell-init files Those categories are interactive-only by design and are simply not part of this mode. This is what makes --all-safe -y acceptable in a cron job. Since 1.1.0 the mode also runs a startup assertion that aborts with a BUG: message if any protected runtime directory ever leaks into its target list, so a future regression fails loudly rather than deleting something it should not.

-y / --yes auto-confirms cache deletions. It is only valid with --all-safe; the interactive modes ignore it by policy. linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -y means you will not see the decisions until afterwards The allowlist and staleness gate still apply, but you review the log after the run. A standalone all-safe run does not write the walkthrough's JSON session report. For a first run, inspect a --scan and an --all-safe --dry-run first.

By default --all-safe prunes eligible cache files whose atime and mtime are both older than --days (default 100). Extracted packages and versioned tools are handled as whole units under their own idle rules. The human output reports selected results; use the dry run to inspect proposed paths before deletion. linux-cleanup --all-safe -y # 100-day threshold linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -d 30 # more aggressive linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --purge-all # gate off — full wipe --purge-all in a cron job is a poor combination Unattended plus no staleness gate means a Gradle wrapper distribution or Playwright browser bundle can disappear the week before you need it, with nobody watching. Keep --purge-all for deliberate, before-reimaging runs.

linux-cleanup --install-cron This schedules --all-safe -y for Sundays at 03:00 and appends output to ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log. See Alias and cron for the exact entry and how to remove it. If you write the crontab entry yourself, use an absolute path — cron's minimal PATH will not find a ~/.local/bin install: 0 3 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --no-report --cleanup-logs >>~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log 2>&1 --cleanup-logs removes that run's log. Standalone all-safe runs do not write the walkthrough's JSON session record, so --no-report has no further effect here.
tail -100 ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log If the cron log shows command not found, the crontab is using a bare command name — see Troubleshooting.

--doctor finds runtimes that exist on disk but are not wired into your shell configuration, and offers to add the missing init block. Added in 1.1.0. linux-cleanup --doctor This is the mode for pnpm: command not found when you know perfectly well you installed pnpm.

Doctor never deletes or edits an existing line It appends a canonical init block, and only after you confirm. It does not modify, reorder, or remove anything already in your shell configuration. Shell-init files are additionally protected at the deletion layer: safe_rm refuses any path whose basename is .bashrc, .zshrc, .profile, .bash_aliases or similar, wherever it lives. See Protected paths.

Runtime Detects Appends nvm ~/.nvm present, no NVM_DIR init The standard nvm loader block pnpm ~/.local/share/pnpm present, not on PATH PNPM_HOME export and PATH addition bun ~/.bun present, not on PATH Bun's init block deno ~/.deno present, not on PATH Deno's PATH addition cargo ~/.cargo present, not on PATH . "$HOME/.cargo/env"

An installer writes its init block to a file your shell does not read. ~/.profile is only read by login shells; ~/.bash_profile shadows it when present; a change to ~/.bashrc never reaches a zsh session. The runtime installs fine and then appears to vanish. It also happens after migrating a dotfiles repository between machines, or after switching login shells.
Reload your shell, or the change will not appear to have worked: source ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc Then confirm: command -v pnpm && pnpm --version
--globals works even when a package manager is missing from PATH, by falling back to filesystem inspection. So if the audit lists pnpm globals but pnpm itself is not found, --doctor is the fix.

--editor-ext removes superseded VS Code and Cursor extension versions. When an extension updates, the old version directory often stays on disk. On a machine with many extensions and a few years of updates this accumulates to hundreds of megabytes. linux-cleanup --editor-ext

A version directory is a candidate only when both hold: A newer version of the same extension exists — the current version is never a candidate That older version has been idle for --days or more (default 100) The second condition was added in 1.2.1. Before that, supersession alone was enough, which removed old versions you had loaded recently. Output shows per-version idle days, so you can see why something was kept.
The current version of any extension Extension settings, keybindings, or workspace state Anything in ~/.config — that whole tree is protected Extensions in an editor other than VS Code and Cursor

If VS Code shows a missing-extension banner, reload the window: Ctrl+Shift+P → Developer: Reload Window. The editor is holding a reference to a directory that no longer exists. If an extension is genuinely gone — which would mean the "highest version" detection mis-identified the current one — reinstall it and please report the bug: code --install-extension <publisher>.<name>
The size depends on the superseded versions installed on this machine. Use a scan to inspect the current directory before deciding whether to clean it.
Runs as step 4 of the guided walkthrough, and is included in --all-safe since it only ever removes regenerable, superseded copies.
The staleness gate Modes overview

--globals lists your globally installed packages across npm, pnpm, yarn, bun and deno, and marks each one. Added in 1.1.0. linux-cleanup --globals linux-cleanup --globals -d 180 This mode never deletes anything It prints copy-pasteable uninstall commands and stops. You decide what to run. Global packages are exactly the kind of thing that breaks a workflow when removed by surprise, so the tool refuses to remove them for you.

Verdict Meaning recently used Modified or accessed within --days. Leave it needed by: <pkg> Another global declares it as a dependency. Removing it breaks that one STALE — safe to uninstall Idle past the threshold and nothing else depends on it "Safe to uninstall" means safe from the perspective of the other globals on your machine. It cannot know about a shell script, a CI job, or a habit of yours that calls the binary. Read the list before acting.

Globally installed packages are never deleted by any cleanup mode. ~/.local/share/pnpm, ~/.npm, ~/.yarn, ~/.bun/install/global and ~/.deno/bin are on the exact-match protected list specifically to keep them safe — a lesson from a real bug where the pnpm cleanup targeted the install root and wiped global packages. See 1.1.0. This audit is the deliberate counterpart: visibility without automation.

Each manager is queried through its CLI when available, and through filesystem inspection when not. So the audit still works on a machine where pnpm was installed but is not currently on PATH — which is often exactly the situation you are trying to diagnose. If a runtime is on disk but not wired into your shell, --doctor is the mode that fixes that.

Doctor — repair a runtime that is installed but not on PATH Protected paths — why globals are never touched
--audit lists the 20 largest entries in $HOME, sorted by size. It deletes nothing and it does not care whether the tool can clean what it finds. linux-cleanup --audit

--scan measures the categories linux-cleanup knows how to clean. --audit measures your home directory, full stop. That difference is the point. If a 60 GB VM image, a downloaded dataset, or a Steam library is what actually filled your disk, --scan will never mention it and --audit will put it at the top of the list. --audit --scan Scope Everything in $HOME Only cleanable categories Answers What is using my disk? What can this tool reclaim? Writes a JSON session report No No Deletes Never Never

linux-cleanup --audit # what is big? linux-cleanup --scan # what can this tool reclaim? If the audit's top entries appear in the scan, the tool can help. If they do not, you have learned something more useful — the space is somewhere this tool does not go, and you can deal with it directly. Common large things linux-cleanup will not clean: VM images and container storage (~/.local/share/libvirt, ~/.local/share/docker) Game libraries (Steam, Lutris) Datasets, model weights, media libraries Anything in ~/Documents, ~/Pictures, ~/Music, ~/Videos — all protected
du -sh ~/.local/share/* | sort -rh | head -20 du -sh ~/* | sort -rh | head -20 --audit is the fast first pass; du narrows it down once you know where to look.
Scan — what the tool can reclaim Reclaim the most space
--menu prints a numbered list of every category and runs the one you pick. Use it when you know what you want and do not need the ten-step tour. linux-cleanup --menu # or: -m, -i, --interactive

Menu Walkthrough Order You choose Fixed, ten steps Scope One category per selection Everything, in sequence Loops Returns to the menu afterwards Runs to the end Report Per action One session report Best for Targeted cleanup First runs, full sweeps The safety model is identical. Every category behaves exactly as it does in the walkthrough — the allowlist, the staleness gate and per-target confirmation all apply. Picking a personal-data category from the menu still gives you per-entry prompts, and --yes still has no effect on it.
documents.s: How it differs from the walkthrough

documents.t: linux-cleanup --menu -d 30 # 30-day threshold for whatever you pick linux-cleanup --menu --purge-all # staleness gate off linux-cleanup --menu --no-color # plain output

--tui is the same menu rendered as a whiptail or dialog box. It needs one of those installed; --menu needs nothing beyond bash and works over any connection, including a dumb terminal or a ssh -T session where a full-screen dialog would misbehave.

--node-modules finds node_modules directories in projects you have not touched for --days or more, and offers each for deletion. The space available depends on the projects present on this machine. linux-cleanup --node-modules # 100-day default linux-cleanup --node-modules -d 90
This mode requires per-project confirmation and ignores --yes. It is not part of --all-safe and cannot be run unattended. See Guard 3.

It scans your project roots for node_modules directories whose containing project has been idle past the threshold, and reports each with its size and idle days. Nested node_modules inside an already-listed directory are not counted separately. Project roots are configurable via project-roots.txt under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME (default ~/.config). See Environment variables.

node_modules is the most reliably regenerable thing on a developer machine — yarn install or npm install rebuilds it from the lockfile. Two caveats worth knowing before you accept everything: Two ways this can still cost you A patched dependency. If you edited a file inside node_modules directly rather than through patch-package or a yarn patch, that edit exists nowhere else. It is not in any registry and not in your lockfile. No lockfile, no network. Reinstalling needs the registry to be reachable and the lockfile to be present. A project with no committed lockfile may not resolve to the same dependency tree — and an air-gapped machine may not resolve at all. Neither is common, and neither is detectable by the tool. If either applies to a project in the list, decline that one.
The project source — only the node_modules directory inside it Lockfiles, package.json, or anything else in the project Projects touched within the threshold Anything on the protected-path list

linux-cleanup --node-modules -d 30 Lowering the threshold widens the candidate list. At 30 days you will start seeing projects you are still occasionally working on, so read the list rather than accepting in bulk — the cost of a mistake is a reinstall, which is minor but not free.
This runs as step 5 of the guided walkthrough, with the same per-project prompts.
Reclaim the most space Safety guards

linux-cleanup has one entry point and picks its mode from a single flag. Running it with no flag gives you the guided walkthrough. Modes are mutually exclusive — pass one. Options like --days and --yes combine with them.

These modes do not delete cleanup targets. They may still write a local log, and the release check may read a public record when online. Mode Flag Shows Scan -s --scan Every cache category with current sizes Home audit --audit The 20 largest entries in $HOME Globals audit --globals Global npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/deno packages List targets --list-targets Every path the tool can touch, plus the protected list Self-test --self-test Dependency, syntax and safety-guard checks Version -V --version Version and author

These modes can delete cleanup targets. --yes skips the batch confirmation only for --all-safe; other modes keep their own prompts. Mode Flag Behaviour Walkthrough (default) -w Ten guided steps, prompt before each Menu -m --menu Numbered menu — pick one category TUI -t --tui The same, as a whiptail/dialog dialog All-safe -a --all-safe Every regenerable cache in one pass Editor extensions --editor-ext Superseded VS Code / Cursor versions System cleanup --system apt, journal, snap, /tmp, page cache — needs sudo

Personal or project data. These ignore --yes and require per-entry confirmation. See Guard 3. Mode Flag Finds Stale personal files -p --stale Large idle files in ~/Downloads and configured unprotected roots Partial downloads --partials .fdmdownload, .crdownload, .part node_modules finder --node-modules Project dependency dirs idle N+ days

Mode Flag Purpose Reports --reports List, convert, view past session reports Export --export FMT ID Non-interactive conversion Doctor --doctor Repair broken shell-init for nvm, pnpm, bun, deno, cargo Speed diagnosis --speed Measure pressure and startup work; optional fixes ask separately Feedback --feedback Bug-report instructions, optional mailto draft Debug bundle --debug-bundle Package latest log + report into a tar.gz Install alias --install-alias Add a cleanup shell alias Install cron --install-cron Weekly --all-safe -y, Sundays 03:00 Uninstall alias / cron --uninstall-alias --uninstall-cron Remove either

Goal Mode First time using the tool --self-test, then --scan, then --all-safe --dry-run Free space now, with control (default walkthrough) Free space now, no prompts --all-safe -y One specific category --menu or --tui Weekly unattended maintenance --all-safe -y via --install-cron Maximum reclaim before reimaging --all-safe -y --purge-all Find what is eating the disk --audit then --scan Old side projects piling up --node-modules command not found after install --doctor

Option Default Effect -d N --days N 100 Staleness threshold. Lower is more aggressive --purge-all off Disables the staleness gate — full wipe -y --yes off Auto-confirm regenerable caches. Only with --all-safe --no-report off Skip the JSON report. Logs still written --cleanup-logs off Delete this run's log at the end. Reports always kept --no-color off Disable ANSI colour. NO_COLOR also honoured -n --dry-run off Walk a selected cleanup without deleting; local log and update-check state may still be written --json-events off NDJSON for --scan or non-interactive --all-safe --yes Full detail: CLI flags and the modes matrix.

--partials finds abandoned partial-download files and offers them for deletion. These are the placeholder files a browser or download manager writes while transferring, and forgets to clean up when the transfer is interrupted. linux-cleanup --partials

Extension Written by .crdownload Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Edge, Vivaldi .part Firefox, wget, aria2 .fdmdownload Free Download Manager A partial file holds however many bytes arrived before the transfer died — sometimes a few kilobytes, sometimes most of a multi-gigabyte ISO.
Per-file confirmation, --yes ignored, not part of --all-safe. See Guard 3.

A partial file may still be resumable — but usually is not Resuming needs the original download session: the browser's download-manager entry, the source URL, and a server that supports range requests. If the browser has been restarted or the download entry cleared, the partial is unresumable and is pure waste. The file itself is never independently useful — a half-downloaded archive does not open. So the practical question is only whether you still intend to resume it. Check before accepting a large one: Open your browser's downloads page and look for a paused or failed entry matching the filename If there is one, resume it there rather than deleting the partial If there is not, the partial is orphaned and safe to remove

A download running right now also has a .crdownload or .part file. The tool has no way to distinguish an in-progress transfer from an abandoned one. Deleting an active partial breaks the transfer in progress — so check your downloads page if you are unsure, or run this mode when nothing is downloading.
documents.s: An active download will show up here

documents.t: Step 6 of the guided walkthrough.
Stale personal files — the related interactive mode Deletion is permanent

--stale finds files over about 10 MB in ~/Downloads and configured unprotected roots that have been unused for --days or more, and offers them for deletion one at a time. linux-cleanup --stale # or: -p linux-cleanup --stale -d 180 # only files idle 180+ days Personal files can be irreplaceable ~/Downloads and your configured unprotected roots hold whatever you put there — including, sometimes, the only copy of something that matters. The tool cannot tell an installer you will never open again from a document you have not needed yet. It does not try. Read every candidate.

Per-file or per-range confirmation is mandatory. --yes is ignored here and always will be, and this mode is not part of --all-safe. See Guard 3. The candidate list is printed in full before anything is asked, so running the mode and declining everything is a legitimate way to audit those directories.

Three conditions together: It lives in a configured personal root — by default ~/Downloads; protected roots such as ~/Desktop are ignored It is larger than roughly 10 MB Both atime and mtime are older than --days (default 100) Personal roots are configurable through personal-roots.txt under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME (default ~/.config). See Environment variables. Why ~/Downloads is not on the protected list It cannot be — cleaning it is the entire point of this mode. The allowlist protects ~/Documents, ~/Pictures, ~/Music and ~/Videos precisely so that the one directory it does reach is the one you expect. If you keep things you care about in ~/Downloads, move them somewhere protected — that is the durable fix, and it protects them from more than this tool.
documents.s: What makes a file a candidate

documents.t: Each entry shows path, size and idle days. Worth pausing on: Pattern Consider Installers, ISOs, .deb/.AppImage Usually safe — re-downloadable Anything you produced rather than downloaded Keep, or move somewhere protected Client or work deliverables Keep. Downloads is a bad home for them Media with no obvious source Investigate before accepting Archives you never extracted Check the contents first

linux-cleanup --audit # what is actually large in $HOME linux-cleanup --stale -d 365 # only genuinely ancient files Starting at 365 days and working down gives you a short, obvious list first. Once that is clear, lower the threshold.
Step 7 of the guided walkthrough. Skipping it there with s and running it separately later — when you have time to read carefully — is a reasonable habit.
Deletion is permanent Partial downloads — the related interactive mode Home audit — find what is large first

The guided walkthrough writes a JSON session record to ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-<timestamp>.json, unless --no-report or --dry-run is set. Other modes do not create that record. Existing records are not auto-deleted. Markdown and HTML are optional conversions produced on demand. linux-cleanup --reports # interactive manager linux-cleanup --export both latest # non-interactive conversion

Section Holds schema_version Currently 1 credits Tool name, version, homepage, licence, author details meta Timestamps, duration, host, user, mode, staleness threshold, log path, launcher disk Filesystem usage before and after memory Memory usage before and after steps One entry per step: number, title, status, bytes freed totals Total bytes reclaimed, human-readable total, steps run and skipped Full field-by-field reference: Report schema.

linux-cleanup --reports Lists past sessions and lets you view one, convert it to Markdown or HTML, open the HTML in a browser, or delete it. Conversion options are hidden when jq is not installed — see below.

Non-interactive, for scripts and habits: linux-cleanup --export both latest # Markdown + HTML from the newest record linux-cleanup --export html all # every record to HTML linux-cleanup --export md 3 # record #3 to Markdown Argument Accepts Format md, html, both Identifier a record number, latest, or all Output lands beside the JSON with the same timestamp in the filename. The HTML is self-contained — embedded CSS, dark-mode aware, no external assets — so it can be emailed or archived as a single file.

JSON is always written; conversion is the optional part Without jq, a walkthrough can still produce its JSON record. Only Markdown and HTML export are unavailable, and step 10 of the walkthrough records itself as skipped (jq missing). sudo apt install jq # Debian / Ubuntu sudo dnf install jq # Fedora / RHEL sudo pacman -S jq # Arch The generated HTML escapes every JSON-derived value through jq's @html filter, so a malformed input cannot inject markup into the rendered page.

The JSON is meant to be read by tools: # Total reclaimed by the most recent session jq '.totals.total_reclaimed_human' ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | tail -1 # Every step that actually ran, most recent session jq '.steps[] | select(.status == "ran") | {title, freed_bytes}' \ "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)" # Reclaim across every recorded session jq -s 'map(.totals.total_reclaimed_bytes) | add' ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json

These records are never deleted automatically — not even by --cleanup-logs, which only removes the current run's log file. To thin them yourself: find ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/ -name 'report-*' -mtime +90 -delete Skip generation entirely for a single run with --no-report; the log is still written.

A session record is a step summary, not a backup It records steps and disk observations, not a complete list of every removed file. It contains none of the removed content, and nothing in it can restore anything. Its value after an unwanted deletion is helping you identify what to restore from your own backup, or re-download. See Recovery.
Report schema — every field Output paths — where files land Recovery — using a session record after a surprise
--scan lists paths and their current sizes without deleting files. It is a first look at the machine. Use a dry run of the selected cleanup mode to see proposed actions. linux-cleanup --scan

The scan prints a table of cache and build-tool roots: package managers, browsers, Gradle, test runners, Android tooling and other configured locations. It also lists partial downloads, likely duplicate downloads, large stale personal-file candidates and a few system observations. It does not run package-manager cleanup or ask for sudo. A listed cache root's size covers everything currently in that root. It is not the amount the tool will remove. The chosen mode, staleness threshold, current use and refusal rules determine what stays. The scan writes a local session log. It does not write the walkthrough's JSON session report.

Check a path you do not recognise. A symlink can point somewhere different from its visible name; inspect it with realpath before a cleanup. The protected-path guard also resolves symlinks before it deletes. Personal-file candidates appear for review only. Routine --all-safe cleanup does not select them. To preview cache cleanup: linux-cleanup --all-safe --dry-run A dry run walks that mode without deleting. It may still write a local log and update-check state. A real deletion has no undo.
documents.s: Read the paths before choosing a mode

documents.t: linux-cleanup --scan --json-events > scan.ndjson The version 1 event stream goes to stdout; human text goes to stderr. It can contain full local paths. Keep it on this machine and use the exit code to distinguish a complete run from an interrupted stream.

Command Question it answers --list-targets Which configured paths can a mode target or refuse? --audit Which entries in $HOME are largest, whether or not a cleanup mode covers them? --globals Which global runtime packages are installed? --self-test Do required commands, syntax and safety-guard assertions pass? Read Preview before deleting for the sequence, then CLI flags for mode options.

--speed reports where the machine is spending time. It reads thermal counters, CPU, memory and I/O pressure, heavy processes and boot information. It can also find containers, services and login apps that start by themselves. linux-cleanup --speed --dry-run linux-cleanup --speed The dry run reports the changes it would ask about without applying them. A normal run asks separately before a proposed change; the default answer is No. --yes does not authorise these fixes. Some accepted fixes stop a container, disable a service or change a user login setting. They do not remove cache files, but they affect what starts next time. The CLI prints an undo command after an applied change. A sudo prompt may appear for a system service change. A finding is a measurement or a condition, not proof that a particular app is faulty. Read the named process or service and decide whether you need it before accepting a change. For missing runtime commands in shell startup, use the separate Doctor mode. For disk space, start with a scan.

--system requests sudo before it starts, then asks about each system step. It uses apt and dpkg directly for package work, so the full mode is for Debian and Ubuntu. Other distributions may run the journal or /tmp parts but the package commands will fail; see Distro support. linux-cleanup --system --dry-run linux-cleanup --system A dry run prints proposed commands without removing cleanup targets or changing settings. It may still write a local log and update-check state. Review it before a real run, which has no undo.

Step What the source runs after confirmation Default apt sudo apt autoremove --purge -y, then sudo apt clean Yes Journal sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=100M Yes Snap Eligible disabled revisions through sudo snap remove Yes Kernels Lists installed linux-image-* packages through dpkg No deletion /tmp sudo find /tmp -mindepth 1 -atime +7 -delete Yes Page cache sudo sync, then sudo sysctl -q -w vm.drop_caches=3 No The journal target is 100 MB and the /tmp age is 7 days; neither follows --days. The Snap step keeps a disabled rollback revision until its replacement has met the configured age threshold, unless --purge-all is used. The kernel listing is informational; apt may remove superseded kernel packages in its earlier step. The /tmp step relies on access times. If the filesystem does not record them reliably, the tool skips age-based deletion. Page-cache eviction frees RAM, not disk, and can make subsequent reads slower while cache fills again.

The mode caches sudo credentials while it runs so it can issue its separate commands. Do not start a system cleanup unless you are prepared to review those commands. --speed has separate optional fixes that can also request sudo; system mode is not the only sudo-capable path in the CLI. The size recovered depends on the machine. A disk-space change measured after the run may also include writes from other processes. Read the log for the commands the tool attempted.
Preview before deleting Safety guards Distro support
--tui renders the category menu as a full-screen whiptail or dialog box. Added in 1.3.0. Same behaviour as --menu, different presentation. linux-cleanup --tui # or: -t, -g, --gui

Selecting an entry drops out of the dialog, runs that category with the normal CLI output and prompts, then returns to the menu. So the dialog is a launcher — the actual confirmations are still the standard text prompts, and every safety guard is unchanged. The TUI also carries an About dialog showing version, contact details, licence and the privacy guarantee.

Needs whiptail or dialog. If neither is present, the tool prints a per-distro install hint and falls back to the regular CLI menu — it does not fail. sudo apt install whiptail # Debian / Ubuntu sudo dnf install newt # Fedora / RHEL sudo pacman -S libnewt # Arch whiptail ships inside the newt / libnewt packages on RPM and Arch systems, which is why the package name does not match the command name. This is the only place the tool detects your distro The install hint above is distro-aware. Nothing else in linux-cleanup is — notably --system assumes Debian/Ubuntu.
--tui needs a terminal that can render a full-screen dialog. Over a constrained connection, inside a CI log, or in a ssh -T session without a TTY, use --menu instead — it needs nothing beyond bash.
