Running linux-cleanup with no flags starts the guided walkthrough: ten steps through every cleanup category, each asking before it does anything. It is the recommended way to use the tool interactively. linux-cleanup # or: linux-cleanup -w / --walkthrough

# Step Deletes Notes 1 Package-manager caches Regenerable yarn, npm, npx, pnpm, pip, composer, bun, deno 2 Application caches Regenerable Browsers, Gradle, Cypress, Playwright, Zoom, editor VSIX 3 Developer-tool data Stale only Android AVDs, pub-cache, Dart analysis, flatpak 4 Editor old extensions Stale + superseded VS Code / Cursor 5 Stale node_modules Interactive Projects idle past the threshold 6 Partial / orphan downloads Interactive .crdownload, .part, .fdmdownload 7 Personal stale files Interactive Large idle files in ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop 8 System cleanup (sudo) System apt, journal, snap, /tmp, page cache 9 Final size audit Nothing Read-only summary 10 Generate readable report Nothing Markdown / HTML export — needs jq Steps 5, 6 and 7 are the interactive-only ones. They cannot be auto-confirmed, and step 7 is the only step in the whole tool that can remove something genuinely irreplaceable.

Two levels of confirmation. Per step, you choose what to do with the whole category: Key Effect a Run this step. This is the default — Enter selects it s Skip this step entirely q Quit the walkthrough now, keeping progress so far Per target, inside a step that you chose to run, each individual item gets a [Y/n] or [y/N] confirmation. The capitalised letter is the default. So a at the step level does not commit you to deleting everything in it — you still see and answer each target.

After each step that ran, the tool prints its measured change and the session total so far. The final summary reports disk free before and after. That figure is measured from df, so it reflects everything happening on the machine — if a build ran during your session, the reported recovery can be lower than the sum of the steps, or even negative. That is not a bug; see Troubleshooting.

q at any step prompt, or Ctrl-C at any point, ends the session cleanly: Earlier deletions remain permanent; inspect the log for the steps attempted before interruption Ctrl-C exits with code 130, which the crash trap deliberately ignores, so no crash bundle is written Steps not reached are recorded as skipped in the report

The walkthrough writes a JSON report to ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-<timestamp>.json unless --no-report or --dry-run is set. It contains per-step status and bytes freed, disk and memory before/after, and session totals. Full field list: Report schema. Step 10 optionally converts it to Markdown and HTML. That step needs jq; without it the step is recorded as skipped (jq missing) and the JSON is still written. linux-cleanup --no-report # skip JSON generation; logs still written

linux-cleanup -d 30 # 30-day staleness threshold instead of 100 linux-cleanup --purge-all # disable the staleness gate entirely linux-cleanup --no-color # plain output linux-cleanup --cleanup-logs # delete this run's log at the end --purge-all changes what step 1–4 delete With the staleness gate off, cache steps wipe their targets in full rather than pruning idle files. That includes Gradle wrapper distributions, Playwright browsers and Cypress binaries you may still want. The pre-run banner states which strategy is active.

linux-cleanup has no undo. This page is about working out what was removed and what your real options are. Stop writing to the disk first If something irreplaceable was deleted and you intend to attempt file-carving recovery, stop using the filesystem now. Every write reduces the chance of recovering unlinked data. That applies only to the genuinely irreplaceable categories. For a cache, skip it — just let the tool re-fetch.

A run can leave a local log. A guided walkthrough can also leave a JSON session record unless reporting was disabled. Neither is a complete per-file deletion record or a backup. # The most recent session log less "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cleanup-*.log | head -1)" # The latest walkthrough record, if one exists jq '.' "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)" To search retained logs for a specific path: grep -rn 'the-filename-you-are-missing' ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/ No match does not prove the tool left that file alone. A helper may report a whole cache directory or a command rather than each file, and --cleanup-logs can remove a run's log. Check the selected mode and target roots too. Narrow to a single session's steps: jq '.steps[] | select(.status == "ran")' \ "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)"
Refusals are logged too. If you find a line like this, nothing was deleted: ✗ REFUSE: protected path: /home/you/Documents/notes See Protected paths.

documents.t: What was deleted Recovery Package-manager cache Automatic. The next install re-downloads it Browser cache Automatic. Rebuilds as you browse Gradle cache or wrapper distro Automatic. Next build re-fetches — expect a slow first build Cypress / Playwright binaries Re-run the install step for that tool node_modules yarn install or npm install in the project Android AVD Recreate in Android Studio. The profile config is gone; the system image re-downloads Editor extension version Reload the editor window; reinstall if genuinely missing apt cache, journal, snap revisions Regenerate on their own. Nothing to do Personal file from ~/Downloads Only from your own backup, or re-download from the source Partial download Not recoverable. Restart the download

# In the affected project yarn install # or: npm install / pnpm install # Test-runner binaries npx cypress install npx playwright install # Flutter flutter pub get Nothing here needs the tool's involvement — you are just letting each tool do what it does on a cold cache.

Realistically, in order: Your own backup. Timeshift, Borg, restic, rsync snapshot, cloud sync — whatever you run. This is the only reliable answer. The original source. A downloaded file can be downloaded again. Check your browser history for the URL. A sync service's trash. Dropbox, Nextcloud, Google Drive and similar keep deleted files server-side for a retention window. If the directory was synced, look there. File-carving tools — extundelete, testdisk, photorec. These work on unlinked inodes and are a long shot on a busy filesystem, especially SSDs with TRIM enabled. Unmount the filesystem first, or work from a live USB, and never write recovered data back to the same device. Be honest with yourself about step 4 On a mounted, actively-used SSD with TRIM, carving usually recovers nothing. It is worth attempting only for something genuinely important, and only after you have stopped writing to the disk.

Change Effect Run --scan before every cleanup You see the outcome while it is still hypothetical Move valuables out of ~/Downloads ~/Documents and ~/Desktop are protected Skip step 7 in the walkthrough Personal files then need a deliberate separate run Raise the threshold: -d 365 Only genuinely ancient files become candidates Never use -y outside --all-safe on a trusted machine -y cannot touch personal data, but you see decisions only afterwards Set up a real backup The only thing that makes any deletion recoverable

If a deletion happened inside a protected path, or a current editor extension version was removed, or anything else contradicts the documented guards — that is a bug worth reporting. linux-cleanup --debug-bundle linux-cleanup --feedback Include the log and a walkthrough record if one exists. See Send a bug report.

Logs are still written --cleanup-logs off Delete this run's log at the end. Records are always kept -n --dry-run off Walk the selected mode without deleting files or changing settings. Scan and dry run answer different questions --scan reads the current paths and sizes. --dry-run walks the selected cleanup and shows proposed actions without deletion. See Preview before deleting.

Most-used, with the full list separately: Variable Effect NO_COLOR Any non-empty value disables colour LINUX_CLEANUP_LOG_DIR Override the log directory LINUX_CLEANUP_REPORTS_DIR Override the session-record directory LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME Parent for logs, records and feedback bundles

Code Meaning 0 Clean run 2 Argument parse error or unsupported event-stream mode 3 An older version blocked by the release record 130 Aborted with Ctrl-C 143 Terminated by SIGTERM other Unexpected — writes a crash bundle Full table and the crash-trap logic: Exit codes.

Every environment variable linux-cleanup reads. All are optional. Variable Default Effect NO_COLOR unset Any non-empty value disables ANSI colour. The cross-tool standard from no-color.org. Same as --no-color CLEANUP_NO_COLOR 0 linux-cleanup-specific colour switch. Set to 1 to disable colour here only LINUX_CLEANUP_LOG_DIR ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/ (npx / npm) or <repo>/logs/ (clone) Where session logs go. Created if missing LINUX_CLEANUP_REPORTS_DIR ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/ or <repo>/reports/ Where JSON session records go. Created if missing LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME unset — falls back to the parent of the log dir Parent for logs/, reports/ and feedback/ together LINUX_CLEANUP_NPX unset Internal. Set to 1 by the Node launcher. Do not set it yourself LINUX_CLEANUP_LAUNCHER unset Internal. The Node launcher sets node; the desktop app sets desktop, which skips the CLI's own update check because the app runs its own (since 2.1.0). Do not set it yourself XDG_CONFIG_HOME ~/.config Where personal-roots.txt and project-roots.txt are looked up

LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME is the single lever that moves everything — logs, records and feedback bundles: export LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME="/mnt/secure/linux-cleanup" linux-cleanup --scan The directory is created, the mount is not The tool creates logs/, reports/ and feedback/ beneath the path you give it. It does not create or verify the underlying mount point. Point this at an unmounted path and output lands on the underlying filesystem instead — quietly. Verify the target is mounted and writable before relying on it. For finer control, LINUX_CLEANUP_LOG_DIR and LINUX_CLEANUP_REPORTS_DIR override individually and take precedence over the data home.

export NO_COLOR=1 # everything on this machine, all tools export CLEANUP_NO_COLOR=1 # only linux-cleanup linux-cleanup --no-color # only this invocation CLEANUP_NO_COLOR exists for the case where you want colour from every other tool and plain output from this one — typically when piping its output somewhere that mangles escape sequences.

Two files under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME (default ~/.config) control which directories the personal and project scanners walk: File Used by Default roots personal-roots.txt --stale ~/Downloads; protected roots such as ~/Desktop are ignored project-roots.txt --node-modules Your project directories One path per line. This follows the XDG Base Directory specification, so setting XDG_CONFIG_HOME relocates both. Adding a root to personal-roots.txt widens what can be deleted The personal scanner is interactive-only, so nothing is removed without your per-file confirmation — but a root you add is a directory whose contents will start appearing in candidate lists. The path allowlist still applies and still wins: adding ~/Documents here does not make it deletable.

NO_COLOR=1 linux-cleanup --scan > /tmp/scan.log The standalone scan does not create the walkthrough's JSON session report. Check the exit code when scripting it, or use --json-events for structured output.

PATH, except to detect which optional tools are installed USER and LOGNAME, except to annotate the log header Your shell history, aliases or configuration — --doctor is the only mode that reads shell-init files, and only to check whether a runtime is wired in Any remote or network-provided configuration. There is none If $HOME is unset the script aborts immediately rather than guessing. See Troubleshooting.
Output paths — where files actually land CLI flags
linux-cleanup follows the Unix convention: 0 is success, anything else is a problem. Some non-zero codes are expected and deliberately not treated as crashes.

Code Meaning Crash bundle 0 Clean run. Every requested action completed or was declined No 1 Generic failure — an invariant was violated. Rare Yes 2 Argument parse error. Help is printed No 3 Update required by the public release record No 127 Command not found — a required dependency is missing Yes 130 Aborted with Ctrl-C (SIGINT) No 137 Killed by SIGKILL — usually the OOM killer or kill -9 Yes 139 Segfault. Should not happen in pure bash Yes 143 Terminated by SIGTERM No any other non-zero Unexpected internal failure Yes An unknown flag exits 2 before cleanup. --dry-run is supported; it walks the selected mode without deleting files. See Preview before deleting.

The EXIT trap added in 1.3.0 evaluates in this order: Exit code is 0, or the script set its internal completion sentinel → no bundle Exit code is 130 (Ctrl-C) or 143 (SIGTERM) → no bundle. A user-initiated stop is not a crash Exit code is 2 (argument parse) → no bundle. The script printed help and stopped on purpose Anything else → write crash-<timestamp>.tar.gz to ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/ The bundle contains the active session log, the most recent JSON record, and a short system manifest. It stays on your machine — nothing is transmitted. The tool prints the path so you can review it and decide whether to email it. See Send a bug report.

if linux-cleanup --scan; then echo "scan succeeded" else case $? in 2) echo "bad flag" ;; 127) echo "missing dependency — run --self-test" ;; 130) echo "user aborted" ;; *) echo "unexpected failure — check ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/" ;; esac fi

linux-cleanup --all-safe -y --no-report --cleanup-logs >>~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log 2>&1 || \ echo "linux-cleanup exited $?" | mail -s "cleanup failed on $(hostname)" you@example.com Exit code 127 from a cron job almost always means the crontab used a bare command name and cron's minimal PATH could not find it. Use an absolute path — see Troubleshooting.

The bundle's manifest records the exit code. The common ones: Code Usual cause 137 Out-of-memory killer. Typically a find over an enormous tree 141 SIGPIPE — a pipe closed early, often a tee or pager exiting 139 Segfault — should never occur here; report it 127 Missing dependency. Run --self-test to identify it

--json-events writes newline-delimited JSON to stdout. Human text and prompts go to stderr, with a local copy in the session log. The stream stays on this machine; it can contain full local paths. Consumers should not upload those paths as part of account or analytics data. The flag supports --scan and --all-safe --yes. An all-safe run needs --yes so a machine client cannot pause at a prompt. Add --dry-run to preview the all-safe action without deleting files. A local log and update-check state may still be written. Other modes return exit code 2. linux-cleanup --scan --json-events > scan.ndjson linux-cleanup --all-safe --yes --dry-run --json-events > preview.ndjson Every complete event has v: 1, a type and ts (Unix milliseconds). Consumers should reject a higher v and ignore unfamiliar fields on version 1. The mode ID is a string: scan or allsafe. Event Fields Meaning plan version, dry_run, profile, sections[] First event; one section for the selected mode. A section has id, title, stamp, sudo, deep. disk phase, total_kb, free_kb, purgeable_kb, snapshots, snapshot_note Disk sample before and after the mode. Unsupported estimates are null. section_start id, title, stamp The selected mode started. item id, path, kb, action, unique, age_days, reason A read-only scan result or a path selected by a cleanup helper. report reads only, delete is a proposed action during a dry run and a completed helper action in a real run, skip is a refusal. kb is truncated to whole KiB. progress id, done, total The one selected mode is at 0/1 or 1/1. It is a mode boundary, not a per-file percentage. error id, message A failure or refusal reported by the CLI. section_result id, status, freed_kb, items, reason Status is completed or failed. Byte and item totals remain null until the CLI can distinguish its own writes from other disk activity. summary attempted, completed, skipped, failed, freed_kb, disk_free_before_kb, disk_free_after_kb, elapsed_s, reports, log, dry_run Last event after a completed mode. The two free-space samples are observations, not a claim of bytes recovered by this process. The stream begins with plan and ends with summary on a completed run. An interrupted process or a failed update requirement may leave no summary; treat that as an incomplete run and use the exit code and stderr. A rejected argument may emit an error event and exit 2 before the plan. Existing text output and exit codes are unchanged when the flag is absent. The event stream complements the local JSON session report. A dry run writes no session report. A consumer can use item.path to explain a local decision, then discard it instead of syncing it to a server. When --cleanup-logs removes the session log, summary.log is null.

All output lives under one data root. Which root depends on how you installed the tool, and both can be overridden.

$DATA_HOME/ ├── logs/ │ ├── cleanup-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.log # one per session │ └── cron.log # appended by the weekly cron ├── reports/ │ ├── report-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.json # guided walkthrough record, unless disabled │ ├── report-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.md # created by --export md │ └── report-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.html # created by --export html └── feedback/ ├── debug-bundle-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.tar.gz # created by --debug-bundle └── crash-<YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS>.tar.gz # created automatically on a crash

Installed via $DATA_HOME npx linux-cleanup ~/.linux-cleanup/ npm install -g linux-cleanup ~/.linux-cleanup/ git clone The clone directory itself The difference is deliberate. npx runs the package from a temporary npm cache directory that gets evicted, so writing output there would lose it; ~/.linux-cleanup/ persists across runs. A clone is already a permanent location, so output stays beside the source. Override either with LINUX_CLEANUP_DATA_HOME, or the log and record directories individually.

Path Auto-cleaned Notes logs/cleanup-*.log Only with --cleanup-logs That flag deletes this run's log at finish. Past logs stay logs/cron.log Never Never rotated. Rotate it yourself if it grows reports/*.json Never The durable audit trail reports/*.md, *.html Never Created on demand, removed on demand feedback/*.tar.gz Never You decide when they are no longer needed --cleanup-logs is the only automatic deletion the tool performs on its own output, and it only ever touches .log files.

Log and bundle size depends on the paths and events in a run. Inspect what has accumulated before deleting old records. To thin older files deliberately: find ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/ -name 'cleanup-*.log' -mtime +90 -delete find ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/ -name 'report-*' -mtime +90 -delete Rotating the cron log: mv ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log.old touch ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log

Files are owned by the invoking user. Inspect their effective modes with stat on your machine; the tool's configured directory modes and the process umask both matter. Avoid sharing a log or bundle without reading it first.

Logs and bundles contain your paths A session log names every path touched, which means it contains directory names from your machine — project names, and sometimes filenames from ~/Downloads. That is local-only and never transmitted, but review a bundle before emailing it: tar -tzf ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/debug-bundle-*.tar.gz See Send a bug report. Nothing here contains file contents — only paths, sizes and timestamps. These are records of what happened, not copies of what was deleted. See Recovery.

These are the paths linux-cleanup refuses to delete. The refusal is unconditional — there is no flag that overrides it, including --purge-all. Every candidate is resolved with realpath before the check, so a symlink pointing into a protected directory is refused on the resolved path, not the link. Verify against your own install rather than trusting this page Lists change between versions, and second-hand descriptions of this tool circulate with directories that are not actually protected. linux-cleanup --list-targets # the lists as your build sees them linux-cleanup --self-test # asserts the guard fires on known paths

The guard is built from three lists with different matching rules. The distinction matters — it is what lets ~/.npm/_cacache be cleaned while ~/.npm itself is untouchable. List Matches Purpose Protected paths The path and everything beneath it Personal data, credentials, configuration Protected exact Only that exact path Package-manager install roots Protected basenames Any file with that name, anywhere Shell-init and history files

Refused as a path or as any child, except where noted. Path Children also refused / — (root itself) /home No — only the exact path /root No — only the exact path /etc Yes /boot Yes /usr Yes /var No — only the exact path /lib No — only the exact path /sbin No — only the exact path /bin No — only the exact path $HOME No — the home root itself, so a bare $HOME can never be wiped /proc and /sys are not on this list No cleanup target goes anywhere near them, but the allowlist does not name them explicitly. Some descriptions of this tool claim it does. It does not.

Refused along with everything inside them. Path Holds ~/Documents Documents ~/Pictures Images ~/Music Audio ~/Videos Video ~/Desktop Desktop contents ~/Public Shared files ~/Templates Document templates ~/Downloads is deliberately NOT protected It cannot be — cleaning large, long-idle files there is a feature (Stale personal files). What protects it instead is Guard 3: interactive-only, per-file confirmation, and --yes ignored. If you keep anything irreplaceable in ~/Downloads, move it into a protected directory. That is the durable fix.

Path Holds ~/.ssh SSH keys and known hosts ~/.gnupg GPG keyring ~/.config Application configuration (very broad) ~/.gnome GNOME settings ~/.mozilla Firefox profiles ~/.thunderbird Thunderbird profiles ~/.claude Claude Code state ~/.local/share/claude Claude Code data Two paths commonly claimed as protected are NOT ~/.password-store (pass) and ~/.aws (AWS credentials) do not appear on the protected list in the source. Some write-ups of this tool state that they do. In practice no cleanup target points at either, so neither is at risk during normal operation — but do not rely on the allowlist to defend them. If you want that guarantee, verify with --list-targets on your own install first. Note that ~/.mozilla being protected does not stop Firefox cache cleanup: the cache lives under ~/.cache/mozilla, a different tree.

Matched exactly — children remain cleanable. This is what preserves your globally installed packages while still allowing the regenerable cache inside each install root to be pruned. Ecosystem Paths pnpm ~/.local/share/pnpm and its global, bin, nodejs npm ~/.npm, ~/.npm-global, ~/.npm-global/lib, ~/.npm-global/lib/node_modules yarn ~/.yarn, ~/.config/yarn/global bun ~/.bun, ~/.bun/install, ~/.bun/install/global and its node_modules, ~/.bun/bin deno ~/.deno, ~/.deno/bin Node version managers ~/.volta, ~/.volta/bin, ~/.nvm, ~/.nvm/versions, ~/.fnm Rust ~/.cargo, ~/.cargo/bin, ~/.rustup Go ~/go, ~/go/bin This list exists because of a real defect: before 1.1.0 the pnpm cleanup targeted ~/.local/share/pnpm — the install root — and removed globally installed packages along with the pnpm binary itself. The fix narrowed the target to ~/.local/share/pnpm/store and added this list so the mistake cannot recur. --all-safe additionally asserts at startup that none of these ever appear in its target list, aborting with a BUG: message if one does.

Refused by filename, in any location, regardless of the path leading to it: .bashrc · .bash_profile · .bash_login · .profile · .bash_logout · .zshrc · .zshenv · .zprofile · .zlogin · .zlogout · .bash_aliases · .bash_history · .zsh_history · .inputrc · .dircolors · .config · .local This is a last-ditch guard. It exists so a future bug that somehow introduced a shell-init file into a target list still cannot delete it.

✗ REFUSE: protected path: /home/you/Documents/notes ✗ REFUSE: unsafe path: '/home/you' ✗ REFUSE: shell-init / history file: /home/you/.bashrc A refusal is correct behaviour, not an error to work around. If a cache you want cleaned is being refused, the cause is almost always a symlink landing somewhere protected — fix the symlink, not the tool. See Troubleshooting.

The guided walkthrough writes a JSON record with "schema_version": 1, unless --no-report or --dry-run is set. The standalone --scan does not write this report. For a machine-readable scan, use --scan --json-events; that stream has a different structure. Older documentation describes a different structure Some material — including a reference page inside the source repository — describes a shape built around schema (a string like linux-cleanup/report/v1) with tool, session and categories objects. The tool does not emit that. A parser written against it will fail on every real file. The structure below is what modules/walkthrough.sh writes. Confirm on your own machine: jq 'keys' "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)"

{ "schema_version": 1, "credits": { }, "meta": { }, "disk": { "before": {}, "after": {} }, "memory": { "before": {}, "after": {} }, "steps": [ ], "totals": { } } Key Type Holds schema_version number Currently 1. Reject anything you do not recognise credits object Tool identity, licence and author meta object Session context — when, where, how, with what settings disk object Filesystem usage before and after memory object Memory usage before and after steps array One entry per step attempted totals object Session summary

{ "tool": "linux-cleanup", "tool_version": "2.1.0", "tool_homepage": "https://aoneahsan.com", "tool_license": "MIT", "author": { "name": "Ahsan Mahmood", "email": "aoneahsan@gmail.com", "website": "https://aoneahsan.com", "linkedin": "https://linkedin.com/in/aoneahsan" } } Present so a record is self-attributing wherever it ends up. Nothing here reflects your machine.

Key Type Holds tool string Always linux-cleanup tool_version string The version that wrote the record. Gate consumer logic on this started_at string Session start timestamp finished_at string Session end timestamp duration_seconds number Wall-clock duration host string hostname output user string $USER mode string The mode that ran — walkthrough, scan, allsafe, system, and so on stale_days number The --days threshold in force log_file string Absolute path to this session's log launcher string How it was invoked — bash for a direct run via_npx number 1 when run through the npm launcher, 0 otherwise stale_days is worth capturing: it is the difference between a run that pruned at 100 days and one that ran with -d 30, and it explains why two sessions on the same machine reclaimed different amounts.

Both hold a before and an after snapshot, taken at session start and end. disk carries filesystem fields — filesystem, size, used, available and use percentage — derived from df. memory carries the equivalent from the system's memory report. after minus before is not purely your cleanup These are whole-machine measurements. A build, a package update or a browser running during the session moves them too, which is why a reported recovery can be lower than the sum of the steps — or negative. See Troubleshooting.

An array, one entry per step attempted, in order: { "n": 1, "title": "Package-manager caches", "status": "ran", "freed_bytes": 13315108864 } Key Type Holds n number 1-based step number title string Human-readable step name status string ran, skipped, skipped (quit), or skipped (jq missing) freed_bytes number Bytes reclaimed by this step. 0 when skipped skipped (quit) marks the steps after you pressed q — useful for telling a deliberate stop from a step you declined individually.
Key Type Holds total_reclaimed_bytes number Sum across steps total_reclaimed_human string The same, formatted steps_run number Steps with status ran steps_skipped number Steps with a skipped status

LATEST="$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)" jq '.totals.total_reclaimed_human' "$LATEST" jq '.meta | {mode, stale_days, duration_seconds}' "$LATEST" jq '.steps[] | select(.status == "ran") | "\(.title): \(.freed_bytes)"' "$LATEST" # Reclaim across every session on record jq -s 'map(.totals.total_reclaimed_bytes) | add' ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json

No JSON Schema file ships with the tool. A structural check: jq -e 'has("schema_version") and .schema_version == 1 and has("meta") and has("steps") and has("totals")' \ ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json Prints true per valid file.

Writing a consumer: Branch on schema_version. Treat an unfamiliar value as unparseable rather than guessing Treat unknown keys as additive. Fields have been added within version 1 and may be again Use meta.tool_version for behaviour that differs between releases Do not assume every mode fills every section. Read-only modes produce fewer steps Expect total_reclaimed_bytes to be negative occasionally. It is a df delta, not a sum of deletions

linux-cleanup applies up to four independent gates before any deletion. A path must clear every gate that applies to it. This page explains what each gate is, why it exists, and what it does not cover. The guards are the entire safety model. There is no backup and no undo behind them.

Always on. Cannot be disabled, and no flag overrides it. Before any removal, the target is resolved with realpath and rejected if it lands on or inside a protected path. Because resolution happens first, a symlink cannot smuggle a path through: if ~/.cache/yarn is a symlink into ~/Documents, the resolved path is inside ~/Documents, the guard fires, and the deletion is refused. Three separate lists back this up: List Match style Purpose System roots and personal directories Path or any child /etc, ~/Documents, ~/.ssh, ~/.config, … Package-manager install roots Exact path only ~/.local/share/pnpm, ~/.npm, ~/.cargo, … Shell-init and history files Basename, any location .bashrc, .zshrc, .bash_history, … When the guard fires you see a refusal on stderr: ✗ REFUSE: protected path: /home/you/Documents/notes The exact-match list deserves a note. ~/.npm is protected exactly, which is what allows ~/.npm/_cacache — a child — to be cleaned. That is deliberate: the install root is preserved while the regenerable cache inside it is fair game. The full lists are at Protected paths. What this guard does not do It protects locations, not value. A 40 GB irreplaceable video sitting in ~/Downloads is not covered by the allowlist — ~/Downloads is not a protected path. It is covered by Guard 3 instead. The cleanup modes select named target paths, then the protected-path check refuses dangerous destinations. A path outside the protected list is not automatically safe to remove: inspect each mode's targets and its dry run.

Default: 100 days. Introduced in 1.2.0, extended in 1.2.1. Since 1.2.0 the default strategy is to prune, not wipe. Within a target directory, a file is deleted only when both its atime and its mtime are older than --days. Empty directories left behind are swept up; the directory shell itself stays so the owning tool still finds its layout. Requiring both timestamps matters. mtime alone would delete a file downloaded a year ago and read yesterday; atime alone is unreliable on filesystems mounted noatime or relatime. Requiring both is the conservative reading. For anything that is a tool rather than a cache — Android AVDs, editor extension versions, flatpak user data — 1.2.1 added a second condition on top. Such an asset is removed only when no active software depends on it AND it has been idle past the threshold. Each asset is evaluated as an indivisible unit, so a partial prune cannot leave a half-deleted emulator profile behind. linux-cleanup --all-safe -y -d 30 # more aggressive: 30-day threshold linux-cleanup --all-safe -y # default: 100 days linux-cleanup --all-safe --purge-all # gate OFF — full wipe, pre-1.2.0 behaviour --purge-all disables this guard entirely With --purge-all every target cache is wiped in full regardless of age. That is the behaviour that prompted the gate: it removes Gradle wrapper distributions, Playwright browsers for old release branches, and yarn-cached tarballs of pinned dependencies — each an expensive re-download. It is a legitimate choice before reimaging a machine. It is a poor default for everyday use. The pre-run banner states which strategy is active, so there is never any ambiguity about what is about to happen.

The modes that can touch personal files are interactive by policy: --stale — large, idle files in ~/Downloads and configured unprotected roots --partials — orphaned partial downloads --node-modules — stale project dependency directories --yes does not apply to these modes and never will. --yes auto-confirms regenerable caches only. The tool prints its candidate list, waits for per-entry confirmation, and deletes nothing until you answer. The reasoning is that personal files carry no signal a program can read. Nothing on disk distinguishes an installer you will never open again from the only copy of a document you have not needed yet. The user is the only oracle, so the tool refuses to guess.
documents.s: Guard 3 — Personal data is interactive only

documents.t: --system is the only mode that calls sudo, and it does so for a fixed, enumerated set of operations — each a separate, reviewable invocation, each prompted individually: Operation Prompt default apt autoremove --purge -y and apt clean Yes journalctl --vacuum-size=100M Yes Remove disabled snap revisions Yes List installed kernels — no deletion — Remove /tmp files with atime older than 7 days Yes sync then sysctl vm.drop_caches=3 No The script does not edit /etc/sudoers, and --system asks for each operation. If sudo is unavailable the mode aborts rather than continuing in a degraded state. Two values here are hardcoded and ignore --days: the journal vacuum target (100 MB) and the /tmp age threshold (7 days).

Being explicit about the gaps is more useful than reassurance. Gap What it means No undo Nothing here makes a deletion reversible. See Deletion is permanent. ~/Downloads is not protected It is reachable through the interactive personal-file mode — read the candidates. ~/Desktop is protected. --purge-all removes Guard 2 Guards 1, 3 and 4 still apply; the staleness gate does not. Running as root widens the blast radius The tool is designed to run as a normal user. --system handles the legitimate sudo needs internally. Guards protect paths, not content A protected directory is safe wherever it sits; a valuable file outside one is not. /proc and /sys are not on the protected list Nothing targets them, but the allowlist does not name them either.

npx linux-cleanup --self-test # asserts the guards fire on known paths npx linux-cleanup --list-targets # prints both target and protected lists --self-test is the honest check. It asserts that /, $HOME, ~/Documents, ~/.ssh and /etc are protected and that ~/.cache/yarn is not, then exits non-zero if any assertion fails. Documentation can drift; the assertion runs against the code you actually have.
Protected paths — the complete verified lists Deletion is permanent — the model behind "no undo" What it deletes — the target inventory

linux-cleanup calls rm -rf. There is no undo, no trash directory, no snapshot, and no backup step. Once a path is removed, this tool cannot bring it back, and neither can any flag you pass it. Read this before your first destructive run Deleted files do not go to a trash or recycle bin. There is no --undo, no restore command, and no hidden copy kept anywhere. A local log may help you retrace a run; a walkthrough record summarizes its steps. Neither is a file-by-file backup. If a file was irreplaceable and you had no backup, it is gone. The tool's safety comes entirely from refusing to delete the wrong thing in the first place.

Most of what this tool removes is described as regenerable. That word is doing precise work, and it is worth being exact about what it does and does not mean. It means It does not mean Some other program can recreate the data linux-cleanup can recreate it The next yarn install re-downloads the package The bytes are still on your disk somewhere The browser rebuilds its cache as you browse The deletion is reversible Recreation may need network, time, or both Recreation is free or instant A Playwright browser bundle is regenerable — and re-downloading it takes several minutes and a few hundred megabytes of bandwidth. An offline machine cannot regenerate it at all. Regenerable is a statement about where the data can come from, not about how convenient it is to get back.

Three targets can contain data that is not regenerable. All three are interactive-only, and all three deserve real attention when you are answering prompts. Target Why nothing can bring it back Personal files in ~/Downloads or configured unprotected roots No source to re-fetch from. If it was the only copy, that was the copy. Partial downloads (.crdownload, .part, …) Resumable only by the original browser session, which is usually long gone. Uncommitted work inside a stale node_modules Rare, but a patched dependency you edited in place is not in any registry. The first is the one that costs people data. ~/Downloads is not a protected path — it cannot be, since cleaning it is a core feature — so the only thing standing between a file there and deletion is you reading the candidate list.
documents.s: The categories that are genuinely irreplaceable

documents.t: The design rationale, stated plainly: An undo log is write amplification on the disk you are trying to free. Preserving 20 GB in order to reclaim 20 GB accomplishes nothing. It would create false confidence. A tool that appears reversible invites careless use, and the reversibility would be partial at best — an undo that restores 90% of cases is most dangerous in the other 10%. Prevention is a better investment than recovery. The allowlist, staleness gate and interactive confirmation stop the bad deletion from happening, which is strictly better than undoing it afterwards. This is a reasonable trade for caches. It is a trade you should understand before pointing the tool at ~/Downloads.

If a deletion surprises you, inspect the available local records. Neither is a backup. Artefact Location Contains Session log ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cleanup-<timestamp>.log Human output for the run, unless the log was removed JSON report ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-<timestamp>.json Walkthrough step summary, unless reporting was disabled They can help identify the mode and selected targets, but do not list every deleted file. They contain none of the deleted content. Full procedure: Recovery.

# 1. Confirm the guards work on this install npx linux-cleanup --self-test # 2. See what would be reclaimed — deletes nothing npx linux-cleanup --scan # 3. Run guided, answering 'n' to anything you are unsure about npx linux-cleanup Beyond that: Have a backup of anything irreplaceable. This is true regardless of this tool; it is simply the only thing that makes any deletion recoverable. Never point the personal-file modes at a machine you have not audited. Run --scan first. Keep --all-safe -y for caches on machines you already trust. It cannot touch personal files, but it also shows you nothing until it finishes. Treat --purge-all as a pre-reimage tool, not a daily driver. The one habit worth forming Run --scan before --all-safe, every time. It costs a minute and it is the only step that shows you the outcome while it is still hypothetical.
documents.s: Reducing the risk before you run

documents.t: Recovery — the procedure after an unwanted deletion Safety guards — what prevents the deletion in the first place Preview before deleting — the read-only modes

Start with --scan, then run the cleanup mode with --dry-run. The scan shows paths and sizes without deleting. A dry run walks the selected cleanup and prints the actions it would take, without removing files or changing settings. Both still create a local session log. linux-cleanup --self-test linux-cleanup --scan linux-cleanup --all-safe --dry-run --self-test checks dependencies, Bash syntax and the protected-path guard. Stop if it fails.

--scan lists cache roots, partial downloads, likely duplicate downloads, large stale personal-file candidates and system observations. Its size for a cache root is everything currently there, not the amount that a later cleanup will remove. The 100-day default staleness threshold, current use and mode-specific rules may keep most of it. The scan does not create a JSON session report. If you need a machine-readable scan, use linux-cleanup --scan --json-events. The event stream can include full local paths; keep it on your machine.

--dry-run walks the selected cleanup path and prints proposed actions. For example: linux-cleanup --all-safe --dry-run linux-cleanup --all-safe --yes --dry-run --json-events > preview.ndjson The first command still asks for confirmation, just as a real run would. The second is non-interactive and writes versioned JSON events to stdout; human text goes to stderr. Neither deletes files. A dry run writes no JSON session report. A preview is a snapshot of the current machine, not a promise about a later run. Files may be used, modified or removed between preview and confirmation. The tool has no undo or backup.
documents.s: What does a dry run show?

documents.t: --list-targets prints configured target roots and protected paths without measuring the disk. It helps answer whether a directory is in scope. The protected-path reference describes the refusal rules. Personal-file and project-adjacent modes are separate from routine cache cleanup. Review their candidates individually. --yes applies to --all-safe only; it does not approve personal-file deletion. When the preview matches your intent, choose the mode you want and read its confirmation. A real deletion is permanent.
documents.s: Check the boundary before a real run

documents.t: What it deletes Safety guards CLI flags

linux-cleanup removes selected caches and leftovers permanently. The target depends on the mode. A scan lists paths and current sizes; a dry run walks the chosen cleanup and shows proposed actions. Neither is a backup. linux-cleanup --list-targets linux-cleanup --scan linux-cleanup --all-safe --dry-run The protected-path guard refuses configured personal and system locations after resolving symlinks. Read every proposed path before a real run.

Routine all-safe cleanup can prune these cache roots. Reinstalling a package may need a network download afterwards. Cache Target root Yarn Berry ~/.yarn/berry/cache npm ~/.npm/_cacache npx installs ~/.npm/_npx pnpm store ~/.local/share/pnpm/store pnpm cache ~/.cache/pnpm bun ~/.bun/install/cache deno ~/.cache/deno Composer ~/.cache/composer pip ~/.cache/pip Yarn v1 extracted packages are pruned as whole entries in ~/.cache/yarn. Globally installed packages and the package-manager install roots are separate from these caches.

Routine targets include the configured browser caches, Gradle version units, Cypress and Playwright binaries, and TypeScript watcher cache. A browser or build tool may need to rebuild or download removed material on its next use. The current Gradle distribution and current Android Studio version are kept by their own rules; an eligible old unit is removed whole so a half-deleted installation is not left behind. The mode checks last access and modification before file-level pruning. An unreliable access-time filesystem prevents age-based pruning. --purge-all removes that age guard and requires a separate decision.

The scan can show Android AVDs, Flutter pub cache, Flatpak user data and other large roots. A path appearing in the scan is not a promise that --all-safe will remove it. Read the mode-specific page and the dry-run output to see what a selected mode actually targets. Android emulators and installed Flatpak apps are not routine cache material.
--editor-ext considers superseded VS Code and Cursor extension versions. It requires a newer version and an idle old version; the current version is kept. See Editor extensions.

Stale project node_modules, partial downloads and large stale personal-file candidates use separate interactive modes. --yes does not approve these modes. A partial download or a file in ~/Downloads may be the only copy you have. Read each path and its consequence before confirming.
documents.s: Project and personal files — interactive only

documents.t: --system asks before its apt, journal, Snap, /tmp and page-cache steps. Its package-manager commands use apt and dpkg; they do not adapt to Fedora, Arch or openSUSE. The kernel step lists installed versions; it does not remove one directly. Journal vacuum uses a 100 MB target, and /tmp aging uses 7 days regardless of --days. Dropping page cache affects RAM, not disk space. See System cleanup and Distro support.

The guard refuses root and protected home paths such as ~/Documents, ~/Pictures, ~/.ssh, ~/.config and ~/.claude. The exact list and its exceptions are in Protected paths. --self-test checks selected refusal cases in the installed copy. A real deletion has no undo. Preview before deleting explains the order to use before a cleanup.
Symptom → cause → fix. Run the verify command first; if it matches, apply the fix. If you have lost data rather than hit an error, go to Recovery instead.

✗ REFUSE: protected path: /home/you/Documents/something Cause. The path resolved — after symlink expansion — to somewhere on the protected list. The allowlist blocked it. This is correct behaviour, not a failure. Nothing was deleted. Fix. Find out what resolved where: linux-cleanup --list-targets realpath <the path that was rejected> Almost always a cache symlinked into a protected directory. Fix the symlink, not the tool — the tool is doing exactly its job. There is no override flag, by design. Two related messages: ✗ REFUSE: unsafe path: '/home/you' # bare $HOME or / ✗ REFUSE: shell-init / history file: … # .bashrc, .zshrc and similar

Cause. --tui was run with neither installed. Fix. Install one, or accept the offered fallback to the CLI menu. sudo apt install whiptail # Debian / Ubuntu sudo dnf install newt # Fedora / RHEL sudo pacman -S libnewt # Arch Verify. command -v whiptail, then re-run. See TUI.
documents.s: TUI mode needs whiptail or dialog

documents.t: Cause. --export md, --export html, or a conversion in the reports manager, without jq installed. Fix. sudo apt install jq jq is needed only for conversion. JSON records are still written on every run without it. See Reports.

Cause. A required dependency is missing or shadowed by an incompatible alias. Common on minimal containers that ship BusyBox instead of GNU coreutils. Verify. linux-cleanup --self-test This probes every required command and names the first one missing. Fix. Install your distro's coreutils, findutils and gawk packages. On Alpine: apk add coreutils findutils bash realpath matters most — it is what makes the protected-path check symlink-safe. See Distro support.

Verify. tail -100 ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cron.log crontab -l | grep -i cleanup Cause. command not found in the cron log means cron's minimal PATH (/usr/bin:/bin) cannot see your install. This is the single most common cron problem. Fix. Use an absolute path in the crontab: crontab -e # Change: 0 3 * * 0 linux-cleanup --all-safe -y … # To: 0 3 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/linux-cleanup --all-safe -y … Find the right path with command -v linux-cleanup. Alternatively put a PATH= line at the top of the crontab. See Alias and cron.
documents.s: Cron entry runs but does nothing

documents.t: ✗ $HOME is not set Cause. Running in a context that does not set $HOME — some Docker images, some CI runners. Fix. HOME=/root linux-cleanup --scan Or export it once for the session. The script aborts rather than guessing, deliberately: a wrong $HOME would mean every path check is evaluated against the wrong tree.

Cause. find walking thousands of directories under $HOME. On a spinning disk the first run takes one to three minutes. Verify. Watch the log rather than the terminal: tail -f ~/.linux-cleanup/logs/cleanup-*.log New lines every five to ten seconds means it is working. Fix. Be patient on the first run; later runs are faster thanks to cached directory metadata. If the same path consistently stalls past five minutes, suspect a symlink loop or an unresponsive network or FUSE mount — and report it.

Cause. The reported recovery is a df delta across the whole machine. Another process — a build, a package update, journal rotation, an IDE re-indexing — wrote more during your session than the cleanup reclaimed. This is not a bug, and it does not mean the cleanup failed. Check what the steps themselves reported: jq '.steps[] | select(.status == "ran") | {title, freed_bytes}' \ "$(ls -t ~/.linux-cleanup/reports/report-*.json | head -1)" Fix. Re-run --scan when the machine is quiet to see the real picture.
documents.s: Disk usage grew during the session

documents.t: Cause. Rare. apt clean does not break apt update, but the cleanup may have raced with another apt operation holding a lock. Verify. sudo apt update 2>&1 | tail -20 Fix. sudo rm -f /var/lib/apt/lists/lock /var/cache/apt/archives/lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend sudo apt update Do this only when no apt process is genuinely running — ps aux | grep -i apt first.

Cause. Usually correct behaviour: a superseded version was removed while the editor still held a reference to it. Fix. Reload the window — Ctrl+Shift+P → Developer: Reload Window. Verify the current version is still present: ls ~/.vscode/extensions/ | grep <extension-name> If the current version is genuinely gone, that indicates a bug in the highest-version detection. Reinstall and report it: code --install-extension <publisher>.<name>
documents.s: VS Code reports a missing extension

documents.t: Cause. The script exited non-zero from somewhere unexpected — a backgrounded find killed by the OOM killer, or a broken pipe. Fix. Read the exit code in the bundle's manifest: tar -xzOf ~/.linux-cleanup/feedback/crash-*.tar.gz --wildcards '*MANIFEST*' 137 is the OOM killer, 141 is SIGPIPE, 139 a segfault. See Exit codes. Any of these is worth reporting.
documents.s: A crash bundle appeared but I saw no crash

documents.t: Cause. The shell rc file has not been re-read. Fix. source ~/.bashrc # or ~/.zshrc Or open a new terminal.

Verify. command -v linux-cleanup linux-cleanup --version Cause. An old global install shadowing a newer npx cache, or a stale shell command hash. Fix. npm uninstall -g linux-cleanup npm install -g linux-cleanup@latest hash -r linux-cleanup --version Check the npm package for the current published version. Review the changelog for changes since your installed copy.
linux-cleanup --debug-bundle linux-cleanup --feedback Review the bundle, then email it with a short description of expected versus actual. See Send a bug report.
